boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Hameln entry (capitulation, 20 November 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: the Prussian garrison of the fortress under its commandant, General Schöler, with General Lecoq's corps, and the troops of the King of Holland, of Marshal Mortier and then of General Savary before it, from the joining of Lecoq's corps on 23 October through the investment of 7 November and the summonses and negotiations to the capitulation of 20 November, the mutiny and the French occupation of 21 November. The fortress's preparation from August 1806, Lecoq's march towards the Elbe and back, and the suspension of arms of 16 November, which was not ratified, are context. Nienburg (B377a), which Savary's troops took after leaving Hameln, and Magdeburg (B376c) are outside this entry. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) as 6,000 men under General of Division Savary, and side B (Prussian) as the garrison of 10,000 men with 129 guns under Major General v. Lecoq, which the French forced to capitulate after a 14-day blockade, the garrison then to be led away into captivity. By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner gives the garrison's parts and his own totals (claim side-b-strength), the French letters other estimates (claim side-b-strength-french), and Höpfner and the French letters side A's troops (claim side-a-strength). Bodart's 10,000 is Höpfner's 'almost 10,000' and the top of his 9—10,000, and his 6,000 is Höpfner's 'only 6000' for the enemy (our comparison); but Höpfner's 93, 46, 21 and 15 guns, without the unserviceable ones, make 175 (our arithmetic), not Bodart's 129. Which source Bodart used was not checked. Bodart names Lecoq as the garrison's commander, while Höpfner has Schöler as commandant (claim bodart-commanders). English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 20/11. capitulation of Hameln'; 'the French (6,000 men) under General of Division Savary, after a 14-day blockade, force the Prussian garrison (10,000 men with 129 guns) under Major General v. Lecoq to capitulate, after which the garrison was to be led away into captivity'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) in Höpfner: of infantry there were originally in Hameln the regiment Prinz Oranien and the 3rd musketeer battalions of Kurfürst von Hessen, Hagken, Tschammer and Schenk, of which the first two together numbered only 314 men, 3058 men in all, joined by the invalid companies of the regiments Tschammer, Schenk, Kurfürst von Hessen and Hagken; 181 artillerymen, so that the infantry had to give 3 assistants per gun to make 5 men to serve it; 2 officers and 28 men of the miner corps; and a detachment of 40 horses of the Köhler and Pletz hussars as the fortress's cavalry. Recruits and the replacement men of the regiments Treuenfels and Strachwitz, together about 1000 men, reinforced it at the end of September and the beginning of October, and after the events on the Saale some 1000 stragglers probably also came in, so that the garrison amounted to over 5000 men. On 23 October General Hagken's detachment was drawn into the garrison, and in exchange the 1st battalion of Oranien, 810 men, joined General Lecoq, whose corps thereby reached 4000 men. The protocol of the council that followed General Loison's summons held that a corps of 9000 men must be dearer to the King than so remote a fortress; after the capitulation Höpfner gives the garrison as 9—10,000 men strong, and as almost 10,000.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 349-350, 361 and 376-377; the figures were checked on full-resolution crops. The garrison and Lecoq's corps were at Hameln before the investment, so the claim is tagged inherited. Höpfner names no source for these figures, and gives none for General Hagken's detachment or the invalid companies. Reading the 810-man battalion as taken from the garrison's over 5000 in exchange for Hagken's detachment, the garrison and Lecoq's 4000 make over 8190 without that detachment (our reading and arithmetic); the passages read do not reconcile this with the protocol's 9000 or the later 9—10,000 and almost 10,000. The 9000 is the protocol's figure for the corps to be kept for the King, not a count. English renderings (ours): 'of infantry there were originally in Hameln: the regiment Prinz Oranien, the 3rd musketeer battalions of Kurfürst von Hessen, Hagken, Tschammer and Schenk, of which the first two, however, together numbered only 314 men, 3058 men in all, to which the invalid companies of the regiments Tschammer, Schenk, Kurfürst von Hessen and Hagken were added'; 'of artillery there were 181 men in the fortress, so that 3 assistants per gun still had to be given by the infantry to obtain 5 men to serve it'; 'of the miner corps 2 officers and 28 men were present'; 'a detachment of 40 horses of the Köhler and Pletz hussars formed the cavalry of the fortress'; 'this garrison was reinforced at the end of September and the beginning of October by recruits and by the replacement men of the regiments Treuenfels and Strachwitz, together by about 1000 men, and also after'; 'the unhappy events on the Saale some 1000 stragglers probably also turned up in the fortress, so that the garrison amounted to over 5000 men'; 'this was the state of things when General Hagken's detachment was drawn into the garrison on 23 October, and in exchange the 1st battalion of Oranien, 810 men strong, joined General Lecoq, whose corps thereby reached a strength of 4000 men'; 'in a protocol signed by all it was unanimously declared that the free withdrawal was to be accepted, since in the prevailing circumstances a corps of 9000 men must be dearer to the King than holding so remote a fortress, which must in any case fall in 2 months at the latest; but before the capitulation was concluded an officer was to be sent to the Elbe to convince himself of the truth of the circumstances stated'; 'in all, of the garrison 9—10,000 men strong, about 600 men were taken prisoner, although General Savary's report speaks of 6000 men'; 'so Hameln fell, in a complete state of defence, with a garrison of almost 10,000 men, with stores for a long time — without the great stores of the burghers — into the hands of an enemy only 6000 men strong, who in guns had nothing but 6-pounder cannon and 3 old 30-pounder hanging mortars, which he had first fetched from Rinteln'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), side A's (French) figures: the Emperor wrote to the King of Holland on 22 October that the Prussians did not have 1,500 men of garrison at Nienburg and that he had reason to think they had at Hameln only just what was necessary for the garrison; on 9 November he wrote to Ney that the King of Holland reported 7,000 men at Hameln camped under the walls of the place. Mortier wrote on 13 November that the enemy's forces at Hameln and Nienburg together were estimated at 10,000 men, who could intercept French convoys and detachments if they were not closely observed.
claims.rationale: Side A's letters, read from the page images; the figures were checked on full-resolution crops. Not reconciled with Höpfner's figures or Bodart's (claims side-b-strength, bodart-strength). The garrison and Lecoq's corps were at Hameln before the investment, so the claim is tagged inherited. The passages read do not say whether the King of Holland's 7,000 camped under the walls are Lecoq's corps, which Höpfner has camped at the foot of the Klütberg from 24 October (claim side-b-command), or the whole garrison; Mortier's 10,000 covers Hameln and Nienburg together. English renderings (ours): 'the Emperor to the King of Holland. Dessau, 22 October 1806'; 'the Prussians do not have 1,500 men of garrison at Nienburg on the Weser. I have reason to think that they have at Hameln only just what is necessary for the garrison'; 'the Emperor to Marshal Ney. Berlin, 9 November 1806'; 'the King of Holland informs me that there are at Hameln 7,000 men camped under the walls of the place'; 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 13 November 1806'; 'the enemy's forces both at Hameln and at Nienburg are estimated at 10,000 men; they could intercept our convoys and our detachments if they were not closely observed'.

claims.value: Side A (French): Bodart gives 6,000 men under General of Division Savary. Höpfner: the division Gobert of the Army of the North was set in motion directly against Hameln while the division Michaud marched there from Kassel by Hörter; on 7 November the enemy advanced with a cavalry brigade, a Dutch Guard dragoon regiment and a hussar regiment, the troops at Gr. Berkel belonging to the division Gobert; on 10 November part of Mortier's corps appeared, Mortier having detached a division against Hameln. On the 13th it was learned that the King of Holland's guards and some other regiments had left with him, and that the division of Mortier's corps was said to have left earlier for Hamburg. After a page not read, Höpfner says it was known for certain that the enemy had moved down the Weser with a great part of his forces, and that General Lecoq estimated the enemy left behind at only 6000 men. On the 19th the Prince of Waldeck said that Italian troops had arrived at Pyrmont to reinforce the blockading troops. By Höpfner, Napoleon's order of 13 November to Mortier judged the Dutch corps of about 6000 men sufficient if properly entrenched, and his order of 18 November to Savary said that the 12th light infantry regiment was already on its way from Kassel as reinforcement and that General Lagrange was to be asked to send some cavalry. On the 20th, when the Prussian generals rode to the Wehrberg Warte, a crowd of French officers stood before the house where Savary had dismounted and two dragoon squadrons were drawn up, and on 22 November two more French regiments arrived at Hameln. Höpfner: Hameln fell to an enemy only 6000 men strong. The French letters: on 22 October the Emperor told the King of Holland that he was adding a corps of nearly 12,000 men to the King's army corps, and on 31 October that Mortier had 10,000 men and the King 12,000, together 22,000, much more than the army of Hanover needed. Mortier wrote on 12 November that the King had put at his disposal the divisions of Generals Dumonceau and Michaud, in all about 7,000 men, held back at Hameln the day before by new orders of the King; on 13 November, that the King had kept them before Hameln for some days more and that, unable to delay his march on Hamburg, he was ordering Dumonceau to leave in observation before Hameln and Nienburg the 2nd and 3rd light infantry regiments, the 7th of the line and the 2nd of cavalry, all Dutch troops, weak corps whose return he had not yet obtained, with 10 pieces of ordnance, while Michaud was to join him with his division of the 22nd, 65th and 72nd French infantry regiments and the 2nd Dutch hussars. The 32nd Bulletin, of 16 November: Savary had been charged with the blockade of Hameln with the Dutch division. No passage read gives a return of side A before Hameln at the capitulation.
claims.rationale: Bodart from the frame transcription; Höpfner and the French letters read from the page images, the figures checked on full-resolution crops. The force before Hameln changed during the blockade, as troops arrived and left on the orders of the King of Holland, Mortier and the Emperor, so the phase is left unresolved. Bodart's 6,000 matches Höpfner's 'only 6000', Lecoq's estimate and the 'about 6000' of the order of 13 November as Höpfner gives it (our comparison); the passages read do not show that any of them is a count. Höpfner's divisions Gobert and Michaud and Mortier's divisions Dumonceau and Michaud are kept as named; whether Gobert's division is Dumonceau's is not shown. Höpfner says that as good as nothing about the enemy's movements in western Germany has been communicated from the French side, and the Emperor's orders of 13 and 18 November are known here only from his summary; they were not seen in Foucart. Whether the 12th light, the cavalry from Kassel or the Italian troops arrived before the capitulation is not shown; the two regiments of 22 November arrived after it. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; '[di]vision Gobert of the Army of the North in motion directly against Hameln, while the division Michaud marched there from Kassel by Hörter' (the sentence begins on p. 356, which was not read); 'on 7 November at 1 o'clock Lieutenant Massow, who stood on outpost with 60 dragoons and 10 hussars, reported that the enemy was advancing on the road from Lemgo and that his posts this side of Aerzen were being pushed back by superior enemy cavalry'; 'the enemy soon advanced with a cavalry brigade — a Dutch Guard dragoon regiment and a hussar regiment — and forced the Prussian officers to retreat on Kl. Berkel'; 'it was the division Gobert to which the troops that appeared at Gr. Berkel belonged; the King of Holland was present in person'; 'on 10 November part of Mortier's corps also appeared before Hameln'; 'Marshal Mortier, after leaving small garrisons, had set out by Münden and Göttingen for Hanover to take possession of that country, and had detached a division against Hameln'; 'also on the 13th many movements were seen in the enemy camps, and it was soon learned that with the King of Holland his guards and some other regiments had also left, as the division of Mortier's corps was said to have left the neighbourhood of Hameln earlier and marched on towards Hamburg, since Napoleon had ordered from Berlin under 6 November that Marshal Mortier should work together with Marshals Soult and Bernadotte for the destruction of Blücher's corps and march on Hamburg to oppose the Prussians' crossing there'; 'it was now known for certain that the enemy had moved off down the Weser with a great part of his forces and had almost entirely evacuated the left bank. General Lecoq himself estimated the enemy left behind at only 6000 men. His camp was seen in the area this side of Fischbeck'; 'on the 19th in the afternoon the Prince of Waldeck came to Hameln and told the generals everything he knew of the events in the Prussian army, assured them also that the French had already crossed the Vistula, so that Prussia was irretrievably lost. He further said that Italian troops had already arrived at Pyrmont to reinforce the blockading troops'; 'under 13 November Napoleon had ordered Marshal Mortier now to set about the investment of Hameln in earnest, to have two bridges thrown over the Weser and to arrange for the blockading troops to entrench themselves properly so as to be safe against any sortie; Rinteln was to serve them as a base and supply the guns for the attack; the Dutch corps, about 6000 men strong, seemed sufficient to be safe against the garrison if properly entrenched'; 'under 18 November Napoleon at last directed General Savary from Berlin to leave at once and go before Hameln to take command of the blockading troops; the guns from Rinteln were to bombard the place and so hasten its surrender, the field guns to defend the entrenchments; the 12th light infantry regiment was already on its way from Kassel as reinforcement; the commandant there, General Lagrange, was further to be asked to send off some cavalry; the garrison of Hameln could be granted a capitulation by which it would be prisoners of war, the officers released on parole, but the private soldiers transported to France etc.'; 'on the morning of the 20th Generals Schöler, Hagken and Lecoq and Colonel Heyn, commander of the regiment Oranien, rode with their adjutants under the escort of Lieutenant Santha's hussars to the Wehrberg Warte; General Wedell had received the command in Hameln in the commandant's absence'; 'a crowd of French officers were before the house where General Savary had dismounted; two dragoon squadrons were drawn up;'; 'on 22 November two more French regiments arrived at Hameln with some 10-pounder howitzers, probably taken somewhere in Hesse'; 'so Hameln fell, in a complete state of defence, with a garrison of almost 10,000 men, with stores for a long time — without the great stores of the burghers — into the hands of an enemy only 6000 men strong, who in guns had nothing but 6-pounder cannon and 3 old 30-pounder hanging mortars, which he had first fetched from Rinteln'; 'it will now be necessary to make up for the enemy's movements in western Germany, though it is to be remarked from the outset that as good as nothing about them has been communicated from the French side'; 'the Emperor to the King of Holland. Dessau, 22 October 1806'; 'send me the formation of your army corps, to which I am adding a corps of nearly 12,000 men'; 'the Emperor to the King of Holland. Berlin, 31 October 1806'; 'Marshal Mortier has 10,000 men and you 12,000; you will thus have 22,000 men; that will be much more than you need for the army of Hanover'; 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 12 November 1806'; 'the King has put at my disposal the divisions of Generals Dumonceau and Michaud; they should form in all about 7,000 men. They were held back yesterday at Hameln by new orders of the King'; 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 13 November 1806'; 'the King of Holland has thought fit to keep the divisions Dumonceau and Michaud before Hameln for some days more'; 'being unable to delay my march on Hamburg, I must leave behind these troops that the King had put at my disposal'; 'I am giving orders for General Dumonceau to leave in observation, both before Hameln and before Nienburg, the 2nd and 3rd light infantry regiments, the 7th of the line, the 2nd of cavalry, all Dutch troops'; 'these corps, whose return I have not yet been able to obtain, are weak. I am also leaving him 10 pieces of ordnance'; 'I am charging General Michaud to come and join me, heading for Luneburg, with his division, composed of the 22nd, 65th and 72nd regiments of French infantry, the 2nd Dutch hussars;'; '32nd Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 16 November 1806'; 'General Savary has been charged with the blockade of Hameln with the Dutch division'.

claims.value: Bodart names General of Division Savary as side A's (French) commander and Major General v. Lecoq as side B's (Prussian). Höpfner: Major General and Engineer Brigadier Schöler was appointed commandant of Hameln in May, and Lecoq commanded his own corps, which reached 4000 men on 23 October and camped at the foot of the Klütberg from the 24th; at the Wehrberg Warte Lecoq drafted the capitulation and the commandant signed it, and Schöler refused to let Colonel Caprivi sign as well, since he, the general, was commandant of the town and of the forts. Savary announced his arrival as commander of the besieging corps on the evening of the 19th, sent by Napoleon's order of 18 November to take command of the blockading troops; the 32nd Bulletin, of 16 November, already says that he had been charged with the blockade of Hameln with the Dutch division.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed commanders, read from the frame transcription, with Höpfner and the 32nd Bulletin, read from the page images. Bodart's choice of Lecoq rather than the commandant is kept as printed; the capitulation's text, which would show who signed it, was not seen. The Bulletin is dated two days before the order of 18 November as Höpfner gives it; both are kept (claim side-a-command). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'immediately after the taking of possession Major General Strachwitz commanded in Hameln, but in May Major General and Engineer Brigadier Schöler, an old man of 75, physically and mentally wholly dulled, and therefore slow to decide and extremely anxious, was appointed commandant'; 'this was the state of things when General Hagken's detachment was drawn into the garrison on 23 October, and in exchange the 1st battalion of Oranien, 810 men strong, joined General Lecoq, whose corps thereby reached a strength of 4000 men'; 'on 24 October General Lecoq led his corps into a camp at the foot of the Klütberg, and had its entrenchment begun at once'; 'General Savary now wanted to dictate the points of capitulation at once, but General Lecoq declined this, drafted the capitulation in French himself, and the commandant signed the collated copy after General Lecoq had assured him that there was nothing more to object to'; 'the colonel answered only with tears. When General Savary asked him to sign the capitulation as well, General Schöler refused this with the remark that the colonel did not need to sign, since he, the general, was commandant of the town and of the forts'; 'quite unexpectedly a parlementaire was again announced on the evening of the 19th'; 'it was Captain Charles with a letter from General Savary, in which he announced to the commandant his arrival as commander of the besieging corps, and at the same time expressed his pleasure at the commandant's sensible views of the state of affairs, adding that he nevertheless could not accept the conditions put, since the King of Prussia had not a battalion left and was himself in flight; he wished to settle the rest orally, and left it to them to fix the time and place for it'; 'under 18 November Napoleon at last directed General Savary from Berlin to leave at once and go before Hameln to take command of the blockading troops; the guns from Rinteln were to bombard the place and so hasten its surrender, the field guns to defend the entrenchments; the 12th light infantry regiment was already on its way from Kassel as reinforcement; the commandant there, General Lagrange, was further to be asked to send off some cavalry; the garrison of Hameln could be granted a capitulation by which it would be prisoners of war, the officers released on parole, but the private soldiers transported to France etc.'; '32nd Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 16 November 1806'; 'General Savary has been charged with the blockade of Hameln with the Dutch division'.

claims.value: Höpfner: the division Gobert, with the King of Holland present, drove the Prussian outposts back on 7 November and completed the investment on the left bank that day; on the 8th the enemy reconnoitred the fortress, and on the 9th threw a bridge over the Weser at Ohr under a howitzer battery on the Ohrberg, attacked the post at the Afferde Warte and took up camps at Aerzen, the King's headquarters, and at Ohr on both banks; Rinteln and Hessen-Oldendorf were occupied and Rinteln's guns brought before Hameln. On the 10th part of Mortier's corps appeared and its tirailleurs attacked the covered way at the Mühlen gate, and General of Division Loison brought a letter from the King summoning Lecoq to capitulate in return for free withdrawal and threatening to burn the town in 24 hours; the King approved free withdrawal to the Prussian King's army as the main point, referring the details to Loison and Colonel Brüne. On the 12th, complaining of the detention of General Brack, who by Höpfner had been sent to Hameln on a wholly empty pretext, the King summoned the fortress to surrender in two hours, sending the news of the fall of Magdeburg and Napoleon's army order on Ratkau; he refused to receive Lecoq and demanded that the garrison surrender as prisoners of war, and General Michaud, who commanded the advance guard, wrote that the commandant might send an officer to General Blücher but must then surrender, the garrison becoming prisoners of war. Michaud then announced that the King had left and he had taken the chief command, sending the Bulletins on the capitulations of Prenzlau, Stettin and Küstrin; on the 18th General dü Monceau, who had relieved Michaud, wrote that Napoleon was angered at the Prussian generals' conduct and had ordered that no more capitulation be granted them if they did not surrender at once, and summoned them to negotiate. On the evening of the 19th Savary announced his arrival as commander of the besieging corps and refused the conditions put; at the meeting at the Wehrberg Warte on the 20th he told the Prussian generals in his Emperor's name that the last moment for capitulation had come, added the lie that Glogau and Breslau had already capitulated and wanted to dictate the terms, and the French rejected the 5th article of Lecoq's draft. Mortier wrote on 12 November that he had moved on Hameln by the King of Holland's order to surround it on the right bank and debouched by Hastenbeck on the evening of the 9th, and that on the 10th all the enemy posts were driven into the place and dislodged from the brick fort on the Hamel, at half range from the town. Höpfner: Napoleon had chosen the right man to reach the goal quickly.
claims.rationale: Höpfner and Mortier's letter, read from the page images. These were the steps of side A's commanders before Hameln, so the claim is tagged commander-created; the changes of command followed orders from above (claim side-a-objectives). Dü Monceau's letter came 'on the same day' as the relief of Fort George's garrison on the 18th. Höpfner gives the letters of the King, Michaud, dü Monceau and Savary in summary and cites no document for them in the passages read. The 32nd Bulletin, of 16 November, already has Savary charged with the blockade (claim bodart-commanders), while by Höpfner Napoleon's order sending him is of 18 November and he announced his arrival on the 19th; the dates are kept as given. Mortier's brick fort on the Hamel may be the inundation redoubt that Höpfner has abandoned on the commandant's order in the night to the 10th and occupied by the enemy, who later left it (claim side-b-command); the passages read do not establish it, so Mortier's 'dislodged' and Höpfner's abandonment are both kept. The 'right man' is Höpfner's judgement. English renderings (ours): 'on 7 November at 1 o'clock Lieutenant Massow, who stood on outpost with 60 dragoons and 10 hussars, reported that the enemy was advancing on the road from Lemgo and that his posts this side of Aerzen were being pushed back by superior enemy cavalry'; 'the enemy soon advanced with a cavalry brigade — a Dutch Guard dragoon regiment and a hussar regiment — and forced the Prussian officers to retreat on Kl. Berkel'; 'an enemy column was seen marching towards the Weser and going into bivouacs; and by the occupation of the wood between Berkel and Hemeringen the investment of the fortress on the left bank was completed that same day'; 'it was the division Gobert to which the troops that appeared at Gr. Berkel belonged; the King of Holland was present in person'; 'on 8 November General Lecoq reconnoitred the enemy and the enemy the fortress, which led to an insignificant cannonade'; 'on the 9th the enemy, under the protection of a howitzer battery set up on the Ohrberg, threw a bridge over the Weser at Ohr, for which the boats had been brought downstream'; 'the Prussian post at the Afferde Warte was at once attacked in superior force and, though reinforced from the fortress, pushed back to the barrier'; 'the enemy now took up camps at Aerzen, where the King of Holland's headquarters was, and at Ohr on both banks of the river'; 'Rinteln and Hessen-Oldendorf were occupied by him. In the former place the Hessian garrison had been disarmed and the guns on hand brought before Hameln'; 'on 10 November part of Mortier's corps also appeared before Hameln'; 'an enemy column moved from Rehrsen to the Baßberg and attacked the covered way with tirailleurs, who posted themselves in the gardens and garden houses in front and for a long time kept up their fire with the garrison of the covered way at the Mühlen gate'; 'it was General of Division Loison, who brought a letter from the King of Holland to General Lecoq, in which he summoned him, communicating the position of the various Prussian corps and the surrender of Stettin, Küstrin etc., to capitulate in return for free withdrawal, but in case of refusal threatened to reduce the town to ashes in 24 hours and to lay all the resulting misfortune on the general'; 'he was very kindly received; the King approved the main point: that the garrison could go by the nearest road to the King's army; but referred him for the details to General Loison and Colonel Brüne'; 'it was the enemy General Brack whom Major Beaufort had found with the commandant, and who had been sent to Hameln on a wholly empty pretext'; 'on the ground of General Brack's failure to return, the King of Holland on the 12th sent a parlementaire anew, complained in serious words of that general's detention, and at the same time summoned the commandant and the generals of the garrison to surrender the fortress in two hours if they did not wish to be treated with all severity'; 'to impress them still more, the news of the fall of Magdeburg and the army order in which Napoleon praises the marshals who had pursued Blücher's corps and forced it to capitulate at Ratkau were attached to the summons'; 'at Ohr he met General Michaud, who commanded the enemy advance guard and had him announced to the King of Holland'; 'the King refused to receive the general, and only had him told that the garrison must now in any case surrender as prisoners of war. General Lecoq rejected this condition, but allowed a French officer to accompany him to Hameln with a letter from General Michaud to the commandant, where he was let in in the evening without blindfold'; 'the letter contained nothing but the repetition of the news from the theatre of war already communicated in the morning, with the addition that after such events it was unreasonable still to want to defend the fortress, but that the commandant was permitted to send an officer to General Blücher to convince himself of the truth of what had been communicated, though after this officer's return the fortress must then be surrendered and the garrison become prisoners of war'; 'General Michaud announced by a parlementaire that the King of Holland had left for another destination, and that he, the general, had taken over the chief command. At the same time he sent the Bulletins that announced the unhappy capitulations of Prenzlau, Stettin and Küstrin'; 'on the 18th the garrison of Fort George was relieved by the 1st battalion Oranien and the 3rd battalion of Schenk, since it had many sick from the damp casemates and the fort had no hospital'; 'on the same day, in the afternoon, the Dutch Colonel Stedtmann, who had already been in Hameln once as a parlementaire and spoke German fluently, came to the fortress again with the Prussian officer whom General Lecoq had sent to repay the enemy general the board costs of the captured officers, and brought the commandant a letter from General dü Monceau, who had relieved General Michaud in the command'; 'the letter contained the notice that Napoleon was angered in the highest degree at the conduct of the Prussian generals and had ordered that they be treated with the utmost severity, and that no capitulation be granted them any more if they did not surrender the fortress forthwith'; 'to this was joined the summons to negotiate with Colonel Stedtmann, or to send a plenipotentiary officer with him to Hessen-Oldendorf'; 'quite unexpectedly a parlementaire was again announced on the evening of the 19th'; 'it was Captain Charles with a letter from General Savary, in which he announced to the commandant his arrival as commander of the besieging corps, and at the same time expressed his pleasure at the commandant's sensible views of the state of affairs, adding that he nevertheless could not accept the conditions put, since the King of Prussia had not a battalion left and was himself in flight; he wished to settle the rest orally, and left it to them to fix the time and place for it'; 'at first the Prussian generals refused the meeting, but at last agreed to fix the rendezvous for the 20th at 9 o'clock in the morning at the Wehrberg Warte'; 'the French general received the Prussian generals very brusquely, told them in his Emperor's name that the last moment for capitulation had come, that later nothing more would be ag-'; 'reed to; he repeated the story of all the misfortune that had struck the Prussian state, and added the lie that Glogau and Breslau had already capitulated'; 'General Savary now wanted to dictate the points of capitulation at once, but General Lecoq declined this, drafted the capitulation in French himself, and the commandant signed the collated copy after General Lecoq had assured him that there was nothing more to object to'; 'the 5th article of the draft capitulation, as General Leeoq had drawn it up, commended the officers who belonged to provinces that might be ceded at the peace to the favour of the new monarch with regard to their maintenance in case of invalidity; it was rejected by the French as inadmissible'; 'Napoleon had chosen the right man to reach the goal quickly'; 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 12 November 1806'; 'I moved on Hameln, by the King of Holland's order, to surround that strong place on the right bank of the Weser'; 'on the evening of the 9th I debouched by Hastenbeck; on the 10th, in the course of the day, all the enemy posts were driven back into the place and dislodged from the brick fort situated on the Hamel, at half range from the town'.

claims.value: Höpfner: the commandant, Major General and Engineer Brigadier Schöler, appointed in May, was an old man of 75, physically and mentally wholly dulled, slow to decide and extremely anxious; Colonel Caprivi of the regiment Oranien commanded Fort George. Schöler made difficulties about feeding Lecoq's troops from the fortress. Lecoq camped his corps at the foot of the Klütberg on 24 October and began to entrench it, but on the evening of the 25th resolved to withdraw across the Elbe and on the 26th marched for Münder and Lauenau without informing General Hagken, who had proposed falling on the rear of the troops blockading Magdeburg or marching through Saxony to Silesia; later a council of Wedell and the corps's commanders answered that the corps's departure from Hameln was no longer advisable. On 7 November Captain Hiller was ordered to lead the 1st battalion of Oranien and 2 horse-artillery guns to the Warte at Kl. Berkel to receive the outposts. In the night to the 10th the inundation redoubt was abandoned on the commandant's order; when the enemy later left it, the garrison reoccupied it. After Loison's summons Lecoq held himself bound to accept free withdrawal for his troops, and since Loison would agree to nothing unless the commandant joined, Schöler called all the generals and commanders except Caprivi; their protocol, signed by all, accepted free withdrawal, on Lecoq's condition that an officer first verify the circumstances at the Elbe, and Lieutenant Colonel Hamelberg went to the King of Holland at Aerzen to work out the draft. After Major Beaufort presented the officer corps's remonstrance, the commandant had it declared that there would be no capitulation; Caprivi drew his battalions into the fort and, reprimanded, answered that he would in no case give it up just like that, and Lecoq wrote to the commandant not to be hasty with the surrender. The King's news of the 12th moved both to think of surrender again: Lecoq rode to the enemy camp to seek good terms and rejected surrender as prisoners of war, and, since none of the commanders thought a capitulation justified on Michaud's conditions and Caprivi spoke vehemently against it, the commandant answered that there would be time to think of capitulating when all means of defence were exhausted; it was announced that every capitulation was broken off. On the 13th the commandant promised Caprivi not to negotiate before 20 December; Lecoq quartered his troops in the town and directed the defence with the commandant, 'if what happened can be so called'; the redoubts were abandoned and the coupure in the gorge was given to Caprivi. Though everything seemed to invite a sortie, Höpfner says, they contented themselves with letting Hiller, at his request, try with a hundred volunteers and 16 hussars to bring in guns the enemy had left near Hemeringen. On the 18th Lecoq offered dü Monceau that the commandant would hand over the fortress on 20 December if no relief had come, having first asked Caprivi not to oppose the surrender a second time on that day, to which Caprivi answered that it was still a long way off. The Prince of Waldeck's news of the 19th wholly discouraged the generals, though in public they still prepared a serious defence; that evening the commandant did not want to receive Savary's parlementaire, but Lecoq thought it better to learn at once what the enemy wanted, and the generals, after first refusing, agreed to meet at the Wehrberg Warte on the 20th. There Schöler believed nothing remained but to capitulate, since the enemy stood on the Baßberg only 900 paces from the covered way and was protected against sorties by the inundation, and a bombardment could burn the town and the magazines, which were not bombproof; Lecoq drafted the capitulation and assured the commandant that there was nothing to object to, and the commandant signed; Lecoq told Caprivi everything was settled, and Caprivi answered only with tears. General Wedell, left in command in Hameln, told officers who urged him to oppose the capitulation that it was the business of the commandant and of General Lecoq. Höpfner's judgement: the excuses for the capitulation come to nothing in view of the strong, well-equipped garrison; one would do wrong to have expected greater energy from the 75-year-old commandant, the fault lying, as at Magdeburg, rather in entrusting such posts to such men; Lecoq had every gift for an outstanding defence but seems to have lost all composure, holding every further effort useless and stifling every stirring of sound spirit; and none of the other senior officers had the courage to take the responsibility and put himself at the head of the defence.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 349-377. These were the decisions of the commandant, of Lecoq and of the other commanders at Hameln, so the claim is tagged commander-created. Höpfner cites no document for the council, the protocol or the letters in the passages read, and his judgements of the commanders are his own. Pages 351-352, 362, 366, 368 and 374 were not read, so Lecoq's march and return, the beginning of Major Beaufort's remonstrance, the events on p. 366, the outcome of Hiller's attempt and the officers' letter of the night of the 20th are not restated; the council on p. 353 is not dated in the passage read. English renderings (ours): 'immediately after the taking of possession Major General Strachwitz commanded in Hameln, but in May Major General and Engineer Brigadier Schöler, an old man of 75, physically and mentally wholly dulled, and therefore slow to decide and extremely anxious, was appointed commandant'; 'Colonel Caprivi of the regiment Oranien was appointed commandant of Fort George'; 'General Schöler made difficulties about feeding these troops from the fortress, so that General Lecoq saw himself compelled to levy provisions from the surrounding country in every way, and at the same time to bring in from Beverungen a magazine still on hand'; 'on 24 October General Lecoq led his corps into a camp at the foot of the Klütberg, and had its entrenchment begun at once'; 'when, however, on the evening of the 25th he received news from Hanover that the road through Neustadt, Lüneburg and Artlenburg was still free of the enemy, he suddenly resolved once more to withdraw across the Elbe, and that same night sent Captain Hiller ahead to prepare the march on that line'; 'on the 26th he already set out with the corps for Münder and Lauenau, the advance guard for Neustadt, without informing General Hagken, who had wanted to join him and had proposed falling on the rear of the troops blockading Magdeburg or marching through unoccupied Saxony to Silesia'; 'thereupon General Lecoq called together General Wedell and the commanders of his corps, and put to them the question whether the corps's departure from Hameln was still advisable, since the enemy was already approaching. The answer was in the negative'; 'on 7 November at 1 o'clock Lieutenant Massow, who stood on outpost with 60 dragoons and 10 hussars, reported that the enemy was advancing on the road from Lemgo and that his posts this side of Aerzen were being pushed back by superior enemy cavalry'; 'Captain Hiller at once received the order to lead the 1st battalion of Oranien and 2 horse-artillery guns to the Warte at Kl. Berkel and post them there to receive the outposts'; 'in the night to the 10th the new, though faultily laid-out, inundation redoubt on the right bank of the Weser was abandoned on the commandant's order, since in his opinion it was useless, because the inundation could no longer be drained. The enemy occupied it at once'; 'later the enemy left the redoubt of his own accord, and it was at once reoccupied by the garrison, since it was considered well placed for sending patrols from it to the Afferde Warte'; 'General Lecoq held himself obliged to accept a free withdrawal to the King's army for the troops under his command; but unless the commandant joined in this capitulation, General Loison would agree to nothing'; 'General Schöler therefore called to him all the generals and commanders, with the exception of Colonel Caprivi, and asked their opinion of the proposals made'; 'in a protocol signed by all it was unanimously declared that the free withdrawal was to be accepted, since in the prevailing circumstances a corps of 9000 men must be dearer to the King than holding so remote a fortress, which must in any case fall in 2 months at the latest; but before the capitulation was concluded an officer was to be sent to the Elbe to convince himself of the truth of the circumstances stated'; 'this last condition was set by General Lecoq'; 'Lieutenant Colonel Hamelberg of the regiment Hagken was sent in the evening with his adjutant and with General Lecoq's adjutant, Lieutenant Below, to the King of Holland at Aerzen, to work out the draft of the capitulation'; 'it was the enemy General Brack whom Major Beaufort had found with the commandant, and who had been sent to Hameln on a wholly empty pretext'; 'the major again found some French officers with the commandant, presented the officer corps's remonstrance, and so impressed him by it that he ordered the major to declare that there would be no capitulation'; 'Colonel Caprivi, who about midday had likewise learned by chance that a capitulation was said to have been concluded, had at once drawn his battalions from the town into the fort, and did not obey the commandant's order to come into the town'; 'when the latter thereupon gave him a sharp reprimand in a letter, and declared at the same time that he was commandant of the fortress and the fort only a part of it, the colonel answered that he had acted according to duty and conscience and would in no case give up the fort just like that'; 'even General Lecoq wrote to the commandant that he should by no means be hasty with the surrender of the fortress, since the King perhaps expected a serious defence after all'; 'on the ground of General Brack's failure to return, the King of Holland on the 12th sent a parlementaire anew, complained in serious words of that general's detention, and at the same time summoned the commandant and the generals of the garrison to surrender the fortress in two hours if they did not wish to be treated with all severity'; 'this news moved the commandant, as well as General Lecoq, to think of surrender again'; 'the colonel accepted the invitation, while General Lecoq rode with Captain Hiller and Lieutenant Below to the enemy camp, to obtain good terms of capitulation if possible and at the same time to reconnoitre the enemy'; 'the King refused to receive the general, and only had him told that the garrison must now in any case surrender as prisoners of war. General Lecoq rejected this condition, but allowed a French officer to accompany him to Hameln with a letter from General Michaud to the commandant, where he was let in in the evening without blindfold'; 'to this letter the commandant answered, since none of the commanders considered a capitulation justified under the conditions it contained, and Colonel Caprivi in particular spoke out vehemently against it, that under the conditions given there would still be time to think of a capitulation when all means of defence were exhausted'; 'to quiet the garrison's discontent at the many negotiations, it was formally announced that every capitulation had been broken off and that a serious defence would be made'; 'on the 13th an inventory of all stores was taken, and it turned out that with the most ample rations the provisions would last until 20 December, whereupon the commandant gave Colonel Caprivi the promise, before this'; 'day, not to enter into any negotiation with the enemy'; 'meanwhile the weather had become very bad, and General Lecoq was thereby induced to leave the camp and quarter his troops in the town with the commandant's permission; he himself took quarters in the commandant's building and now directed the further defence together with the commandant, if what happened can be so called'; 'besides the 2nd battalion of Oranien, the 4 companies of the 2nd battalion of vac. Grävenitz were now also moved to Fort George. The redoubts were abandoned as soon as the camp's magazines had been cleared; on the other hand the coupure in the gorge was closed and its defence also entrusted to Colonel Caprivi'; 'the wooded ground up to there was perfectly known, and everything seemed to invite a sortie, given the superiority over the enemy, since the enemy's cavalry was not to be feared in the broken ground'; 'nevertheless they contented themselves with allowing Captain Hiller, at his request, to advance on the left bank of the Weser to try to bring into the fortress some guns that the enemy had left standing near Hemeringen. For this purpose he received a hundred volunteer marksmen of the infantry regiment Lettow and 16 hussars,' (the sentence continues on p. 368, which was not read); 'on the 18th the garrison of Fort George was relieved by the 1st battalion Oranien and the 3rd battalion of Schenk, since it had many sick from the damp casemates and the fort had no hospital'; 'when Colonel Stedtmann, on being asked, named the garrison's captivity as the main condition, General Lecoq, who had command of the French language, as the commandant had not, drew up a letter in which he told General dü Monceau that they had indeed full knowledge of the misfortune of the Prussian army and so counted on no relief, but that they nevertheless meant, in duty, to hold the fortress until all means of defence were exhausted or all provisions consumed; if, therefore, General dü Monceau really intended to spare the town, the commandant would hand over the fortress on 20 December, provided no relief had arrived by then;'; 'before taking this step General Lecoq had spoken with Colonel Caprivi to move him not to oppose the surrender a second time on 20 December, the day on which the provisions would run out, but the latter had answered that that was still a long way off, so there was no need yet to think of surrender'; 'on the 19th in the afternoon the Prince of Waldeck came to Hameln and told the generals everything he knew of the events in the Prussian army, assured them also that the French had already crossed the Vistula, so that Prussia was irretrievably lost. He further said that Italian troops had already arrived at Pyrmont to reinforce the blockading troops'; 'this news, communicated by a prince attached to the Prussian state, wholly discouraged the generals, while in public they still prepared everything for a serious defence and held a conference on it with the artillery and engineer officers'; 'quite unexpectedly a parlementaire was again announced on the evening of the 19th'; 'the commandant did not want to receive him, but General Lecoq thought it better to learn at once what the enemy wanted'; 'at first the Prussian generals refused the meeting, but at last agreed to fix the rendezvous for the 20th at 9 o'clock in the morning at the Wehrberg Warte'; 'all were silent, and as General Savary pressed General Schöler to declare himself, the latter in fact believed that nothing else remained for him but to capitulate, since the enemy stood on the Baßberg only 900 paces from the covered way and was protected against sorties by the inundation, while a bombardment could easily reduce the town, and with it the magazines, which were not bombproof, to ashes, and so on'; 'General Savary now wanted to dictate the points of capitulation at once, but General Lecoq declined this, drafted the capitulation in French himself, and the commandant signed the collated copy after General Lecoq had assured him that there was nothing more to object to'; 'when Colonel Caprivi arrived at the Wehrberg Warte, General Savary went to meet him, but before he could even speak with him, General Lecoq took him into a'; 'window and told him that everything was settled, since in the unhappy circumstances no choice had remained'; 'the colonel answered only with tears. When General Savary asked him to sign the capitulation as well, General Schöler refused this with the remark that the colonel did not need to sign, since he, the general, was commandant of the town and of the forts'; 'on the morning of the 20th Generals Schöler, Hagken and Lecoq and Colonel Heyn, commander of the regiment Oranien, rode with their adjutants under the escort of Lieutenant Santha's hussars to the Wehrberg Warte; General Wedell had received the command in Hameln in the commandant's absence'; 'already in the morning some senior officers had suspected what was going on outside, and had spoken of it with General Wedell at the parole; Major Eller, commander of the 3rd battalion of Hagken, Colonel Renzel, commander of the 3rd battalion of Schenk, and Colonel Oertel, commander of the infantry regiment Lettow, had called on the general to oppose the capitulation, but he had given the answer: "Do you not know Prussian subordination? That is the business of the commandant and of General Lecoq; they have to answer for everything."'; 'all the excuses brought forward for the capitulation that were taken from the fortress's situation come to nothing in view of the strong garrison, well equipped with everything; the reasons based on the political situation of the state were even more reprehensible; the commandant knows no other consideration than the preservation of his fortress'; 'but will one condemn the commandant for his conduct? one would do wrong to have expected greater energy from a physically and mentally wholly worn-out old man of 75 in such shattering circumstances as those of the year 1806'; 'here as at Magdeburg the fault lies far more in such important posts having been entrusted to such men, who were thus given up to disgrace after a long, honourable life'; 'it is otherwise with General Lecoq, who was equipped with all the gifts that could fit a man for an outstanding defence'; 'it seems, however, that the never-imagined, impossible-seeming, terrible fate of the fatherland had taken all composure from him too, so that he held every further exertion useless, every sacrifice still made for the Prussian cause reprehensible; hence his activity in stifling in the germ every stirring of sound spirit'; 'the other senior officers, mostly also very old, had probably become dulled in the monotony of service, for although almost all may have felt the whole shame of such a capitulation, none had the courage to take the responsibility on himself and put himself at the head of the defence' (the sentence's last word, on p. 378, is outside the transcribed passage).
