citations.quote: Als er indessen am Abend des 25. aus Hannover die Nachricht erhielt, daß die Straße über Neustadt, Lüneburg und Artlenburg noch frei vom Feinde sei, faßte er plötzlich noch einmal den Entschluß sich über die Elbe zurückzuziehen, und schickte noch in der Nacht den Hauptmann Hiller voraus, um den Marsch auf genannter Linie vorzubereiten.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 350 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 26. brach er bereits mit dem Korps nach Münder und Lauenau, die Avantgarde nach Neustadt, auf, ohne dem General Hagken Mittheilung zu machen, der sich ihm hatte anschließen wollen und den Vorschlag gemacht hatte, den Blokadetruppen von Magdeburg in den Rücken zu fallen oder durch das unbesetzte Sachsen nach Schlesien zu ziehen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 353 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Darauf berief der General Lecoq den General Wedell und die Kommandeurs seines Korps zusammen, und legte ihnen die Frage vor, ob der Abmarsch des Korps von Hameln noch anräthig, da der Feind bereits im Anmarsch sei. Die Antwort fiel verneinend aus.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 357 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 7. November um 1 Uhr meldete der Lieutenant Massow, der mit 60 Dragonern und 10 Husaren auf Vorposten stand, daß der Feind auf der Straße von Lemgo vorrücke und daß seine Posten diesseits Aerzen von überlegener feindlicher Kavallerie zurückgedrängt würden.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 357 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der Hauptmann Hiller erhielt sogleich den Befehl, das 1. Bataill. von Oranien und 2 reit. Geschütze nach der Warte bei Kl. Berkel zu führen und sie dort zur Aufnahme der Vorposten aufzustellen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 359 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In der Nacht zum 10. wurde die neue, wenn auch fehlerhaft angelegte Inondations-Schanze auf dem rechten Weserufer auf Befehl des Kommandanten verlassen, da sie nach seiner Meinung unnütz war, weil die Ueberschwemmung nicht mehr abgelassen werden könne. Der Feind besetzte sie sogleich.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 360 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Später verließ der Feind die Schanze freiwillig, und wurde sie von der Garnison sogleich wieder besetzt, da man sie für gelegen betrachtete, um von ihr aus Patrouillen nach der Afferder-Warte zu senden.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 361 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der General Lecoq hielt sich verpflichtet, für die unter seinem Befehl stehenden Truppen einen freien Abzug zur Armee des Königs annehmen zu müssen; indessen, ohne daß sich der Kommandant dieser Kapitulation anschlösse, wollte der General Loison auf nichts eingehen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 361 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der General Schöler berief deshalb alle Generale und Kommandeure, mit Ausnahme des Obersten Caprivi, zu sich, und befragte sie um ihre Ansicht über die gemachten Vorschläge.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 361 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: In einem, von Allen unterschriebenen Protokolle, wurde einstimmig ausgesprochen, daß der freie Abzug anzunehmen sei, da unter den obwaltenden Verhältnissen dem Könige ein Korps von 9000 Mann lieber sein müsse, als die Behauptung einer so entlegenen Festung, die in 2 Monaten spätestens doch fallen müsse; jedoch sei vor Abschließung der Kapitulation ein Offizier nach der Elbe zu schicken, um sich von der Wahrheit der angegebenen Umstände zu überzeugen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 361 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Diese letztere Bedingung wurde vom General Lecoq gestellt.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 361 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der Oberst-Lieutenant Hamelberg vom Regmt. Hagken wurde am Abend mit seinem Adjutanten und mit dem Adjutanten des Generals Lecoq, Lieut. Below, nach Aerzen zu dem König von Holland gesandt, um den Entwurf zur Kapitulation zu bearbeiten.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 363 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Es war der feindliche General Brack, den der Major Beaufort beim Kommandanten gefunden hatte, und der unter einem ganz nichtigen Vorwande nach Hameln geschickt worden war.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 363 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der Major fand wieder einige französische Offiziere bei dem Kommandanten, trug die Vorstellung des Offizierkorps vor, und machte dadurch auf ihn solchen Eindruck, daß er dem Major befahl, zu erklären, es würde nicht kapitulirt werden.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 363 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der Oberst Caprivi, der um Mittag zufällig ebenfalls erfahren hatte, daß eine Kapitulation abgeschlossen sein solle, hatte augenblicklich seine Bataillone aus der Stadt nach dem Fort gezogen, und leistete dem Befehl des Kommandanten, nach der Stadt zu kommen, keine Folge.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 363 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Als dieser ihm hierauf in einem Briefe einen scharfen Verweis ertheilte, und zugleich erklärte, daß er Kommandant der Festung, das Fort aber nur ein Theil derselben sei, so antwortete der Oberst, daß er nach Pflicht und Gewissen gehandelt habe und das Fort in keinem Falle ohne Weiteres übergeben werde.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 363 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Selbst der General Lecoq schrieb dem Kommandanten, er möge sich doch ja nicht mit der Uebergabe der Festung übereilen, da der König doch vielleicht eine ernste Vertheidigung erwarte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 363 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Auf Grund des Ausbleibens des Generals Brack sandte der König von Holland am 12. aufs Neue einen Parlamentair, beschwerte sich in ernsten Worten über das Zurückhalten jenes Generals, und forderte zugleich den Kommandanten und die Generale der Besatzung auf, die Festung in zwei Stunden zu übergeben, wenn sie nicht mit aller Strenge behandelt werden wollten.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 363 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Diese Nachrichten bewogen den Kommandanten, so wie den General Lecoq, wiederum an die Uebergabe zu denken.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 364 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der Oberst folgte der Einladung, wogegen der General Lecoq mit dem Hauptmann Hiller und dem Lieut. Below nach dem feindlichen Lager ritt, um wo möglich gute Kapitulations-Bedingungen zu erhalten und zugleich den Feind zu rekognosziren.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 364 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der König schlug es ab, den General zu empfangen, und ließ ihm nur sagen, daß die Besatzung sich jetzt jedenfalls kriegsgefangen ergeben müsse. Der General Lecoq wies diese Bedingung zurück, gestattete aber, daß ihn ein französischer Offizier mit einem Briefe des Generals Michaud an den Kommandanten nach Hameln begleitete, wo er am Abend mit unverbundenen Augen eingelassen wurde.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 364 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Auf diesen Brief antwortete der Kommandant, als keiner der Kommandeurs unter den darin enthaltenen Bedingungen eine Kapitulation gerechtfertigt erachtete, und besonders der Oberst Caprivi heftig dagegen auftrat, daß unter den gegebenen Bedingungen es noch Zeit sein würde, an eine Kapitulation zu denken, wenn alle Vertheidigungsmittel erschöpft sein würden.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 364 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Um das Mißvergnügen der Garnison wegen des vielen Unterhandelns zu stillen, wurde förmlich bekannt gemacht, daß jede Kapitulation abgebrochen sei und man sich ernsthaft vertheidigen werde.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 364 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 13. wurde eine Aufnahme aller Vorräthe angestellt, und es ergab sich, daß bei den reichlichsten Portionen die Lebensmittel noch bis zum 20. Dezember genügen würden, worauf der Kommandant dem Obersten Caprivi das Versprechen gab, vor diesem

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 365 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Tage sich mit dem Feinde in keine Unterhandlung einzulassen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 365 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Das Wetter war mittlerweile sehr schlecht geworden und der General Lecoq sah sich dadurch veranlaßt, das Lager zu verlassen und seine Truppen mit Bewilligung des Kommandanten in der Stadt einzuquartieren; er selbst nahm Quartier im Kommandanturgebäude und leitete nun in Gemeinschaft mit dem Kommandanten die weitere Vertheidigung, wenn man das, was geschah, so bezeichnen will.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 365 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Außer dem 2. Bataillon von Oranien wurden nunmehr auch noch die 4 Kompagnien des 2. Bataill. von vac. Grävenitz nach dem Fort George verlegt. Die Redouten wurden verlassen, sobald die Magazine des Lagers geräumt worden waren; dagegen wurde die Koupüre in der Kehle geschlossen und ihre Vertheidigung dem Obersten Caprivi mit übertragen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 367 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Das bewaldete Terrain bis dahin war vollkommen bekannt, und Alles schien bei der Ueberlegenheit über den Feind zu einem Ausfall einzuladen, da die Kavallerie des Feindes in dem durchschnittenen Terrain nicht zu fürchten war.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 367 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Dennoch begnügte man sich, dem Hauptmann Hiller auf sein Ansuchen zu gestatten, auf dem linken Weserufer vorzugehen, um zu versuchen, einige Geschütze, die der Feind in der Gegend von Hemeringen hatte stehen lassen, nach der Festung zu bringen. Er erhielt zu dem Zweck hundert freiwillige Schützen vom Infanterie-Regmt. Lettow und 16 Husaren,

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 369 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 18. wurde die Garnison des Forts George durch das 1. Bataill. Oranien und das 3. Bataill. von Schenk abgelöst, da sie durch die feuchten Kasematten viele Kranke hatte und das Fort kein Lazareth besaß.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 369 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Als der Oberst Stedtmann auf Befragen als Hauptbedingung die Kriegsgefangenschaft der Garnison anführte, setzte der General Lecoq, der der französischen Sprache mächtig war, der Kommandant aber nicht, ein Schreiben auf, in welchem er dem General dü Monceau sagte: daß man zwar von dem Unglück der preußischen Armee vollständig Kenntniß habe, also auch auf keinen Entsatz rechne, daß man aber dennoch pflichtgemäß die Festung so lange halten wolle, bis alle Mittel der Vertheidigung erschöpft, oder alle Lebensmittel verzehrt seien; wenn daher der General dü Monceau wirklich gesonnen sei, die Stadt zu schonen, so wolle der Kommandant am 20. Dezember die Festung überliefern, sofern kein Entsatz bis dahin eingetroffen sei;

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 370 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der General Lecoq hatte, bevor er diesen Schritt that, mit dem Obersten Caprivi gesprochen, um ihn zu bewegen, sich am 20. Dezember, an welchem Tage die Lebensmittel ausgingen, nicht zum zweitenmal der Uebergabe zu widersetzen, dieser hatte aber geantwortet, bis dahin sei noch lange hin, man brauche daher auch noch nicht an die Uebergabe zu denken.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 370 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 19. Nachmittags kam der Fürst von Waldeck nach Hameln und erzählte den Generalen Alles, was er von den Begebenheiten bei der preußischen Armee wußte, versicherte auch, daß die Franzosen bereits die Weichsel überschritten hätten, mithin Preußen unwiederbringlich verloren sei. Weiter erzählte er, daß italienische Truppen zur Verstärkung der Blokadetruppen bereits in Pyrmont angekommen seien.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 370 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Diese, durch einen dem preußischen Staate zugethanen Fürsten mitgetheilten Nachrichten, entmuthigten die Generale völlig, während sie öffentlich noch Alles zu einer ernsthaften Vertheidigung vorbereiteten und hierzu eine Konferenz mit den Artillerie- und Ingenieur-Offizieren hielten.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 370 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Ganz unerwartet wurde am Abend des 19. abermals ein Parlamentair angemeldet.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 370 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der Kommandant wollte ihn nicht annehmen, doch der General Lecoq meinte, es sei besser gleich zu erfahren, was der Feind wolle.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 370 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Erst schlugen die preußischen Generale die Zusammenkunft ab, bequemten sich aber endlich doch, das Rendezvous auf den 20. um 9 Uhr Morgens bei der Wehrberger Warte festzusetzen.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 372 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Alles schwieg, und da der General Savary in den General Schöler drang, sich zu erklären, so glaubte derselbe in der That, es sei ihm nichts anders übrig geblieben als zu kapituliren, da ja der Feind auf dem Baßberg nur 900 Schritt vom gedeckten Wege entfernt stehe und durch die Inondation gegen Ausfälle geschützt sei, ein Bombardement aber die Stadt und somit auch die nicht bombensicheren Magazine leicht einäschern könne, u. dergl. m.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 372 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der General Savary wollte nun sofort die Kapitulationspunkte diktiren, indessen lehnte der General Lecoq dies ab, entwarf die Kapitulation in französischer Sprache selbst, und der Kommandant unterzeichnete das collationirte Exemplar, nachdem der General Lecoq versichert hatte, daß nichts mehr zu erinnern sei.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 372 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Als der Oberst Caprivi auf der Wehrberger Warte ankam, ging ihm der General Savary entgegen, doch bevor derselbe noch mit ihm sprechen konnte, nahm ihn der General Lecoq in ein

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 373 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Fenster und theilte ihm mit, daß Alles abgemacht sei, da unter den unglücklichen Verhältnissen keine Wahl geblieben wäre.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 373 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Der Oberst antwortete nur durch Thränen. Als der General Savary ihn aufforderte, die Kapitulation mit zu unterzeichnen, wies dies der General Schöler mit dem Bemerken zurück, daß der Oberst nicht zu unterzeichnen brauche, da er, der General, Kommandant der Stadt und der Forts sei.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 371 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Am 20. Morgens ritten die Generale Schöler, Hagken und Lecoq und der Oberst Heyn, Kommandeur des Regmts. Oranien, mit ihren Adjutanten unter der Bedeckung der Husaren des Lieut. Santha nach der Wehrberger Warte; der General Wedell hatte in der Abwesenheit des Kommandanten den Befehl in Hameln erhalten.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 373 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Bereits Vormittags hatten einige höhere Offiziere geahnt, was draußen vorging, und bei der Parole mit dem General Wedell darüber gesprochen; der Major Eller, Kommandeur des 3. Bataill. von Hagken, der Oberst Renzel, Kommandeur des 3. Bataill. von Schenk und der Oberst Oertel, Kommandeur des Inf.-Regmts. Lettow, hatten den General aufgefordert, sich der Kapitulation zu widersetzen, doch hatte dieser die Antwort ertheilt: „Kennen Sie nicht die preußische Subordination? Das ist Sache des Kommandanten und des Generals Lecoq, die haben Alles zu verantworten.“

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 377 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Alle für die Kapitulation beigebrachten Entschuldigungsgründe, aus der Lage der Festung hergenommen, zerfallen in Nichts in Betreff der starken, mit allem wohl ausgerüsteten Garnison; die Gründe, welche auf die politische Lage des Staates fußten, waren aber noch verwerflicher; der Kommandant kennt keine andere Rücksicht als die Erhaltung seiner Festung.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 377 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Will man aber den Kommandanten über sein Verhalten verdammen? man thäte Unrecht, wenn man von einem körperlich und geistig völlig abgelebten 75jährigen Greise unter so erschütternden Verhältnissen, wie die des Jahres 1806, eine größere Energie erwartet hätte.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 377 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Hier wie bei Magdeburg liegt die Schuld bei weitem mehr darin, daß man so wichtige Posten solchen Männern anvertraut hatte und sie somit nach einem langen, ehrenvollen Leben der Schande Preis gab.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 377 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Anders stellt es sich mit dem General Lecoq, der mit allen Gaben ausgerüstet war, die zu einer ausgezeichneten Vertheidigung befähigen konnten.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 377 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Es scheint indessen auch ihm das nie geahnte, für unmöglich gehaltene, entsetzliche Schicksal des Vaterlandes alle Fassung genommen zu haben, so daß er jede weitere Anstrengung für nutzlos, jedes Opfer für verwerflich hielt, das noch der preußischen Sache gebracht wurde; daher seine Thätigkeit, jede Regung von tüchtiger Gesinnung im Keime zu ersticken.

citations.locator: Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 377 (transcribed from the page image)
citations.quote: Die übrigen höhern Offiziere, meist auch hoch bejahrt, waren wohl in der Einförmigkeit des Dienstes stumpf geworden, denn obgleich fast Alle die ganze Schmach solcher Kapitulation gefühlt haben mögen, so hatte doch keiner den Muth, die Verantwortlichkeit auf sich zu nehmen, und sich selbst an die Spitze der Vertheidigung zu

claims.value: Bodart records the capitulation of Hameln on 20 November: the French under Savary forced the garrison to capitulate after a 14-day blockade, after which it was to be led away into captivity; when the capitulation was made known a mutiny broke out among the garrison, ending in the desertion and flight of the greater part of it to the left bank of the Weser, not occupied by the enemy, so that only a weak remnant (600 men) fell into French hands. Höpfner: on the morning of the 20th Generals Schöler, Hagken and Lecoq and Colonel Heyn rode to the Wehrberg Warte, where the commandant signed the collated copy of the capitulation Lecoq had drafted in French: the garrison became prisoners of war, the men to be transported to France and the officers released on parole, the men to keep their knapsacks and the officers their property, and on 22 November at 9 in the morning the garrison was to march out of the Oster gate and lay down its arms; several oral agreements were also made, among them a sum of money to be paid to the commandant for the officers with the longest way home. The generals left at 5 o'clock, and at the gate, the commandant especially, told of the capitulation, so that the soldiers learned of it before the officers, which alone, Höpfner says, brought about the uprising; at 6 the staff officers were ordered to the commandant, and the news spread quickly in the town. The men of the regiment Hagken and of the 3rd battalions broke open the magazines, got drunk and fired their muskets in the streets, especially against the commandant's house; only single companies of Lettow, Oranien and Grävenitz and especially the hussars kept order until the next morning, when the mutineers broke open the bridge gate, threw their muskets and ammunition into the Weser and ran off, and, the left bank not being occupied by the enemy, the men escaped almost all. On the morning of the 21st Savary wrote to Lecoq that the capitulation would be kept, all Prussian officers being answerable for it with property, liberty and life, and called on the commandant to name the rebellious officers; when the French advanced they found the gates unoccupied and took possession of the fortress, and the soldiers still in Hameln were shut in a church and later led away to Rinteln. Savary let the dragoons, hussars, fusiliers and Jäger and Hiller's company of Lettow go home with passes, and on the 21st had several officers arrested who had been pointed out to him as having spoken loudest against the capitulation, releasing them the next day.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome with Höpfner's account, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription); no source read gives a different result. The capitulation's text was not seen; its terms are Höpfner's summary, and he says the 5th article of Lecoq's draft was rejected (claim side-a-command). Höpfner's investment of the left bank on 7 November and the capitulation of the 20th span 14 days counted inclusively, Bodart's 14-day blockade (our arithmetic). Höpfner does not date the occupation in the passages read: Savary's letter came on the morning of the 21st, and he had officers arrested 'still on the 21st', which suggests the French were in Hameln that day, before the march-out agreed for the 22nd (our reading). The officers' letter to which Savary's answered, on p. 374, was not read. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength, and 'after this capitulation was made known a mutiny broke out among the garrison, which ended with the desertion and flight of the greater part of the garrison to the left bank of the Weser, not occupied by the enemy, so that only a weak remnant (600 men) fell into the hands of the French'; 'on the morning of the 20th Generals Schöler, Hagken and Lecoq and Colonel Heyn, commander of the regiment Oranien, rode with their adjutants under the escort of Lieutenant Santha's hussars to the Wehrberg Warte; General Wedell had received the command in Hameln in the commandant's absence'; 'General Savary now wanted to dictate the points of capitulation at once, but General Lecoq declined this, drafted the capitulation in French himself, and the commandant signed the collated copy after General Lecoq had assured him that there was nothing more to object to'; 'the garrison became prisoners of war; the men were to be transported to France, the officers released on parole, the former to keep their knapsacks, the latter their property. On 22 November at 9 o'clock in the morning the garrison was to march out of the Oster gate and lay down its arms'; 'several oral agreements were also made'; 'thus a sum of money was to be paid to the commandant to distribute among those officers who had the longest way home; thus the authorisation of sales of oats that the commandant had made in the last days to pay various bills for shipping freight etc., and so on'; 'at 5 o'clock the generals left the Wehrberg Warte and returned to Hameln. At the gate they were already telling — the commandant especially — that a capitulation had been made, so that the soldiers learned of the misfortune earlier than the officers. This alone brought about the later uprising, and through it made it difficult for a vigorous man to put himself at the head and carry on the defence'; 'at 6 o'clock all the staff officers were ordered to the commandant. The news of the capitulation spread quickly in the town'; 'the men of the regiment Hagken and of the 3rd battalions broke open the magazines, got drunk, scattered or sold the provisions, fired their muskets in the streets, especially against the commandant's house,'; 'only single companies of the regiments Lettow, Oranien and Grävenitz, but especially the hussars, stayed in order, partly at their posts on the ramparts, partly in the town, until the following morning, when the mutineers broke open the bridge gate, threw their muskets and ammunition into the Weser and ran off'; 'now everything dissolved, and since most of the regiments had their cantons in Westphalia and the left bank of the Weser was not occupied by the enemy, the men escaped almost all, and at later enquiries gave themselves out as deserters to escape captivity, while in fact at most 20 men had deserted during the investment. Several burghers and soldiers had been wounded and killed by the musket fire'; 'on the morning of the 21st Captain Charles brought a letter from General Savary to General Lecoq'; 'it contained the declaration, composed in the haughtiest tone, that he was not accustomed to yield to rebellious movements; that it was unheard of for an undisciplined troop to be granted the right to add to a capitulation already concluded conditions that concerned merely its private interest; that the capitulation would be kept and all Prussian officers made answerable for it with property, liberty and life; that on entering, if he met the slightest resistance, he would exercise the greatest severity; that he called on the commandant to name the rebellious officers to him, so that the whole weight of vengeance for such conduct might fall on them'; 'when this letter arrived, resistance was no longer to be thought of, and so when the French advanced they found the gates unoccupied and at once took possession of the fortress. The soldiers still in Hameln were picked up, shut in a church and later led away to Rinteln'; 'to the dragoons, hussars, fusiliers and Jäger, who had always shown themselves equally capable in the few small engagements, and to the company of Captain Hiller of the regiment Lettow, which had stayed at its post until the French entered, General Savary granted, to show them his respect and especially to mock the generals, that they could go home with passes'; 'General Savary had several officers arrested on the 21st who had been pointed out to him as those who had spoken out most loudly against the capitulation, among others the Lieutenants Rhade and Malachowski, but they were released the next day and treated like the other officers'.

citations.quote: 1806 20./11. KAPITULATION von Hameln

Die Franzosen (6.000 M.) unter Div.-Gen. Savary zwingen nach 14tägiger Blokade die preußische Besatzung (10.000 M. mit 129 Geschützen) unter GM. v. Lecoq zur Kapitulation, wonach die Garnison in Kriegsgefangenschaft abgeführt werden sollte.

Nach Bekanntmachung dieser Kapitulation entstand unter der Besatzung eine Meuterei, welche mit der Desertion und Flucht des größten Teiles der Garnison auf das vom Feinde unbesetzte linke Weserufer endete, so daß nur ein schwacher Rest (600 M.) den Franzosen in die Hände fiel.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) lost the fortress and its garrison. Bodart: after the mutiny only a weak remnant (600 men) fell into French hands. Höpfner: in all about 600 men of the garrison of 9—10,000 were taken prisoner, although General Savary's report speaks of 6000; the men escaped almost all, and at later enquiries gave themselves out as deserters to escape captivity, while in fact at most 20 men had deserted during the investment; several burghers and soldiers were wounded and killed by the musket fire; the soldiers still in Hameln were shut in a church and later led away to Rinteln, Savary let the dragoons, hussars, fusiliers and Jäger and Hiller's company go home with passes, and only a few of the officers tried to escape to reach the army in Prussia or Silesia. Hameln fell with stores for a long time, without the great stores of the burghers. Before the capitulation, on 7 November, of the Prussian troops actually engaged, about 200 men strong, the cavalry lost 17 men and the infantry 12 in killed and wounded.

The dead and wounded of the mutiny are not counted. Several burghers and soldiers had been wounded and killed by the musket fire'; 'when this letter arrived, resistance was no longer to be thought of, and so when the French advanced they found the gates unoccupied and at once took possession of the fortress. The soldiers still in Hameln were picked up, shut in a church and later led away to Rinteln'; 'to the dragoons, hussars, fusiliers and Jäger, who had always shown themselves equally capable in the few small engagements, and to the company of Captain Hiller of the regiment Lettow, which had stayed at its post until the French entered, General Savary granted, to show them his respect and especially to mock the generals, that they could go home with passes'; 'of the garrison's officers only a few had tried to save themselves in order to reach the army in Prussia or Silesia; on the contrary several had declared that they held it beneath their dignity to flee without arms and in disguise'; 'so Hameln fell, in a complete state of defence, with a garrison of almost 10,000 men, with stores for a long time — without the great stores of the burghers — into the hands of an enemy only 6000 men strong, who in guns had nothing but 6-pounder cannon and 3 old 30-pounder hanging mortars, which he had first fetched from Rinteln'; 'on 7 November at 1 o'clock Lieutenant Massow, who stood on outpost with 60 dragoons and 10 hussars, reported that the enemy was advancing on the road from Lemgo and that his posts this side of Aerzen were being pushed back by superior enemy cavalry'; 'of the Prussian troops actually engaged, about 200 men strong, the cavalry had lost 17 men, the'; 'infantry 12 men in killed and wounded. claims.value: Bodart places Hameln, a town in Prussia, province of Hanover, on the Weser, 40 km south-west of Hanover. Höpfner: the fortress lay on the right bank of the Weser, fortified on the land side by a detached bastion and 8 bastions, a fausse-braye, a broad and deep main ditch watered by the Hamelbach with small ravelins, covered way and advanced ditch, with lunettes before the detached bastion and the 3 gate ravelins; the water side was only badly defended, by the fortified island of the Werder, and the bridge by a large flèche flanked by 2 small ones. On the right bank the valley heights, namely the Baßberg, came within 1000 paces of the town, and except for the higher ground before the Oster gate the whole valley floor could be flooded by the Hamelbach through a sluice 1600 paces south-east of the fortress. On the left bank the Klütberg, 620 feet high, came within 200 paces of the Weser about 900 paces above the bridgehead, the heights running on in an arc to the north-west until they neared the river again 3600 paces below; on its south-eastern tip lay Fort George, three separate forts, No. I on the summit, No. II lower on the ridge and No. III on the slope to the Weser, with mine galleries before Nos. I and III, and two redoubts half-way secured its link with the bridgehead. The enemy came on 7 November by the road from Lemgo, driving in the posts this side of Aerzen; the occupation of the wood between Berkel and Hemeringen completed the investment on the left bank; the enemy bridged the Weser at Ohr under a battery on the Ohrberg and camped at Aerzen and at Ohr on both banks; a column moved from Rehrsen to the Baßberg and its tirailleurs used the gardens and garden houses before the Mühlen gate; the enemy's camp was later seen this side of Fischbeck, the wooded ground up to it being perfectly known and the enemy's cavalry not to be feared in the broken ground; and the left bank was not occupied by the enemy when the garrison dissolved. Mortier places a brick fort on the Hamel at half range from the town.
claims.rationale: Location and works as described, read from the page images. No plan of Hameln was inspected, and where each work stood is taken only from Höpfner's description; the rest of his description of the Werder and the bridgehead, and the hedges and the coupure on the Pyrmont road, are not restated. Höpfner gives distances in paces and the Klütberg's height in feet; they are not converted. Mortier's brick fort may be the inundation redoubt that Höpfner places 1300 paces from the fortress (claim fortification); the passages read do not establish it. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(town in Prussia, province of Hanover, on the Weser, 40 km south-west of Hanover)'; 'the fortress of Hameln on the right bank of the Weser was fortified on the land side by a detached bastion and 8 bastions, a fausse-braye, a broad and deep main ditch watered by the Hamelbach, with small ravelins, covered way and advanced ditch; lunettes lay before the detached bastion at the lower junction with the Weser and before the 3 gate ravelins'; 'the water side of the fortress was only badly defended, by a fortified island, the Werder'; 'the bridge was defended by a large flèche, flanked by 2 small flèches with ditches and covered way'; 'on the right bank of the Weser the valley heights, namely the Baßberg, come within 1000 paces of the town. Except for the somewhat higher ground before the Oster gate, the whole valley floor could be flooded by the Hamelbach, for which purpose a sluice had been built in the brook 1600 paces south-east of the fortress'; 'on the left bank, about 900 paces above the bridgehead, the Klütberg, 620 feet high, comes within 200 paces of the Weser, and from it the valley heights run on in an arc to the north-west until, 3600 paces below, they come close to the river again'; 'on the south-eastern tip of the Klütberg lay Fort George, consisting of three separate forts: No. I on the summit, No. II lower but still on the ridge, No. III on the slope towards the Weser; all three linked by an open communication, Nos. II and III also by an underground one'; 'before No. I on the hill side and before No. III towards the Weser lay mine galleries'; 'two redoubts lying half-way secured the link between Fort George and the bridgehead'; 'on 7 November at 1 o'clock Lieutenant Massow, who stood on outpost with 60 dragoons and 10 hussars, reported that the enemy was advancing on the road from Lemgo and that his posts this side of Aerzen were being pushed back by superior enemy cavalry'; 'an enemy column was seen marching towards the Weser and going into bivouacs; and by the occupation of the wood between Berkel and Hemeringen the investment of the fortress on the left bank was completed that same day'; 'on the 9th the enemy, under the protection of a howitzer battery set up on the Ohrberg, threw a bridge over the Weser at Ohr, for which the boats had been brought downstream'; 'the enemy now took up camps at Aerzen, where the King of Holland's headquarters was, and at Ohr on both banks of the river'; 'an enemy column moved from Rehrsen to the Baßberg and attacked the covered way with tirailleurs, who posted themselves in the gardens and garden houses in front and for a long time kept up their fire with the garrison of the covered way at the Mühlen gate'; 'it was now known for certain that the enemy had moved off down the Weser with a great part of his forces and had almost entirely evacuated the left bank. General Lecoq himself estimated the enemy left behind at only 6000 men. His camp was seen in the area this side of Fischbeck'; 'the wooded ground up to there was perfectly known, and everything seemed to invite a sortie, given the superiority over the enemy, since the enemy's cavalry was not to be feared in the broken ground'; 'now everything dissolved, and since most of the regiments had their cantons in Westphalia and the left bank of the Weser was not occupied by the enemy, the men escaped almost all, and at later enquiries gave themselves out as deserters to escape captivity, while in fact at most 20 men had deserted during the investment. Several burghers and soldiers had been wounded and killed by the musket fire'; 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 12 November 1806'; 'on the evening of the 9th I debouched by Hastenbeck; on the 10th, in the course of the day, all the enemy posts were driven back into the place and dislodged from the brick fort situated on the Hamel, at half range from the town'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: the fortress was in a very bad state when the Prussians took possession of it, but work began at once; on 13 August came the order to put Hameln in a state of defence, and guns and ammunition arrived gradually from Magdeburg, so that there were 93 guns for the town's fortifications, 46 for Fort No. I, 21 for Fort No. II and 15 for Fort No. III, without the unserviceable ones, with 8400 Centner of powder, mostly already in cartridges, and sufficient iron and lead ammunition; with 181 artillerymen the infantry had to give 3 assistants per gun to make 5 men to serve it. In October the place was amply provisioned for 4000 men for 3 months; Schöler made difficulties about feeding Lecoq's troops from the fortress, so that Lecoq levied provisions in the surrounding country and brought in a magazine from Beverungen. On the 13th an inventory of all stores showed that with the most ample rations the provisions would last until 20 December; only wood was lacking for that time, and Caprivi had it felled and brought in before the forts under a strong line of skirmishers. Fort George's garrison had many sick from the damp casemates, and the fort had no hospital. At the meeting with Savary, Schöler feared that a bombardment could burn the town and the magazines, which were not bombproof. Höpfner: Hameln fell with stores for a long time, without the burghers' great stores, to an enemy who had in guns only 6-pounder cannon and 3 old 30-pounder hanging mortars, first fetched from Rinteln. Side A (French): Rinteln's Hessian garrison was disarmed and its guns brought before Hameln; by Höpfner, Napoleon's orders of 13 and 18 November made Rinteln the blockade's base and the source of the guns for the attack, which were to bombard the place, the field guns defending the entrenchments; Mortier wrote on 13 November that he was also leaving Dumonceau, with the troops left in observation, 10 pieces of ordnance; and on 22 November two French regiments arrived with some 10-pounder howitzers, probably taken in Hesse.
claims.rationale: Höpfner and Mortier's letter, read from the page images, the figures checked on full-resolution crops. Side B's guns and stores were set before the investment; side A's guns came from the commanders' dispositions and the Emperor's orders; one claim carries one phase, so it is unresolved. Höpfner's guns make 175 (our arithmetic), not Bodart's 129 (claim bodart-strength). Old measures are kept as printed. The provisioning for 4000 men for 3 months is dated only 'in October', and the inventory of the 13th does not say for how many men it was reckoned. No passage read counts the stores found at the capitulation. The two regiments with howitzers arrived after the capitulation. English renderings (ours): 'when the Prussians took possession of Hameln the fortress was in a very bad state, but work on it had begun actively at once'; 'on 13 August the order arrived to put Hameln in a state of defence'; 'the necessary guns and ammunition arrived gradually from Magdeburg, so that 93 guns for the town's fortifications, 46 for Fort No. I, 21 for Fort No. II and 15 guns for Fort No. III, without the unserviceable ones, with 8400 Centner of powder, mostly already in cartridges, and sufficient iron and lead ammunition were present'; 'of artillery there were 181 men in the fortress, so that 3 assistants per gun still had to be given by the infantry to obtain 5 men to serve it'; 'in October the place was amply provisioned for 4000 men for 3 months'; 'General Schöler made difficulties about feeding these troops from the fortress, so that General Lecoq saw himself compelled to levy provisions from the surrounding country in every way, and at the same time to bring in from Beverungen a magazine still on hand'; 'on the 13th an inventory of all stores was taken, and it turned out that with the most ample rations the provisions would last until 20 December, whereupon the commandant gave Colonel Caprivi the promise, before this'; 'only wood was lacking for the time given, so the colonel just named had wood felled and brought in in front of the forts under the protection of a strong line of skirmishers'; 'on the 18th the garrison of Fort George was relieved by the 1st battalion Oranien and the 3rd battalion of Schenk, since it had many sick from the damp casemates and the fort had no hospital'; 'all were silent, and as General Savary pressed General Schöler to declare himself, the latter in fact believed that nothing else remained for him but to capitulate, since the enemy stood on the Baßberg only 900 paces from the covered way and was protected against sorties by the inundation, while a bombardment could easily reduce the town, and with it the magazines, which were not bombproof, to ashes, and so on'; 'so Hameln fell, in a complete state of defence, with a garrison of almost 10,000 men, with stores for a long time — without the great stores of the burghers — into the hands of an enemy only 6000 men strong, who in guns had nothing but 6-pounder cannon and 3 old 30-pounder hanging mortars, which he had first fetched from Rinteln'; 'Rinteln and Hessen-Oldendorf were occupied by him. In the former place the Hessian garrison had been disarmed and the guns on hand brought before Hameln'; 'under 13 November Napoleon had ordered Marshal Mortier now to set about the investment of Hameln in earnest, to have two bridges thrown over the Weser and to arrange for the blockading troops to entrench themselves properly so as to be safe against any sortie; Rinteln was to serve them as a base and supply the guns for the attack; the Dutch corps, about 6000 men strong, seemed sufficient to be safe against the garrison if properly entrenched'; 'under 18 November Napoleon at last directed General Savary from Berlin to leave at once and go before Hameln to take command of the blockading troops; the guns from Rinteln were to bombard the place and so hasten its surrender, the field guns to defend the entrenchments; the 12th light infantry regiment was already on its way from Kassel as reinforcement; the commandant there, General Lagrange, was further to be asked to send off some cavalry; the garrison of Hameln could be granted a capitulation by which it would be prisoners of war, the officers released on parole, but the private soldiers transported to France etc.'; 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 13 November 1806'; 'I am giving orders for General Dumonceau to leave in observation, both before Hameln and before Nienburg, the 2nd and 3rd light infantry regiments, the 7th of the line, the 2nd of cavalry, all Dutch troops'; 'these corps, whose return I have not yet been able to obtain, are weak. I am also leaving him 10 pieces of ordnance'; 'on 22 November two more French regiments arrived at Hameln with some 10-pounder howitzers, probably taken somewhere in Hesse'.

claims.value: Side A (French): the Emperor wrote to the King of Holland on 22 October that he had reason to think the Prussians had at Hameln only just what was necessary for the garrison, and on 31 October that Hameln and Nienburg would soon surrender when they learned of their country's disasters; on 9 November he wrote to Ney that the King of Holland reported 7,000 men at Hameln camped under the walls of the place. Mortier wrote on 13 November that the enemy's forces at Hameln and Nienburg were estimated at 10,000 men, and that he had not yet been able to obtain the return of the corps he left in observation. Höpfner: on 8 November the enemy reconnoitred the fortress; Loison, who came with the summons before the attack on the Mühlen gate, was let into the fortress with his whole suite without blindfolds, and the enemy officers with him talked with the numerous burghers gathered before the commandant's building and walked about the town unsupervised, even visiting wine houses; the enemy General Brack, sent to Hameln on what Höpfner calls a wholly empty pretext, was found with the commandant; a French officer who accompanied Lecoq back from the enemy camp with Michaud's letter was let in in the evening without blindfold; and Savary, on the evening of the 19th, expressed his pleasure at the commandant's sensible views of the state of affairs.
claims.rationale: Side A's letters, read from the page images, with Höpfner's. The passages read do not show what side A learned from these visits, or whether it knew of the garrison's stores or of Lecoq's estimate of the blockading force; Savary's 'sensible views' follow Lecoq's offer of 18 November to hand over the fortress on 20 December (claim side-b-command). The garrison estimates are also in claim side-b-strength-french. English renderings (ours): 'the Emperor to the King of Holland. Dessau, 22 October 1806'; 'the Prussians do not have 1,500 men of garrison at Nienburg on the Weser. I have reason to think that they have at Hameln only just what is necessary for the garrison'; 'the Emperor to the King of Holland. Berlin, 31 October 1806'; 'Hameln and Nienburg will not be slow to surrender when they learn of the disasters of their country. Put a small corps of observation before them, without blockading them, to prevent them from making raids in the country'; 'the Emperor to Marshal Ney. Berlin, 9 November 1806'; 'the King of Holland informs me that there are at Hameln 7,000 men camped under the walls of the place'; 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 13 November 1806'; 'these corps, whose return I have not yet been able to obtain, are weak. I am also leaving him 10 pieces of ordnance'; 'the enemy's forces both at Hameln and at Nienburg are estimated at 10,000 men; they could intercept our convoys and our detachments if they were not closely observed'; 'on 8 November General Lecoq reconnoitred the enemy and the enemy the fortress, which led to an insignificant cannonade'; 'even before the attack on the Mühlen gate had taken place, a parlementaire appeared there, who soon afterwards, on the order of the commandant's adjutant, Lieutenant Schmidt, was let into the fortress with his whole suite without blindfolds'; 'it was General of Division Loison, who brought a letter from the King of Holland to General Lecoq, in which he summoned him, communicating the position of the various Prussian corps and the surrender of Stettin, Küstrin etc., to capitulate in return for free withdrawal, but in case of refusal threatened to reduce the town to ashes in 24 hours and to lay all the resulting misfortune on the general'; 'the hussars accompanying the parlementaire had halted before the commandant's building; the enemy officers joined them, talked with the numerous burghers gathered there, then walked about the town unsupervised and even visited various wine houses'; 'it was the enemy General Brack whom Major Beaufort had found with the commandant, and who had been sent to Hameln on a wholly empty pretext'; 'the King refused to receive the general, and only had him told that the garrison must now in any case surrender as prisoners of war. claims.value: Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: on the evening of 25 October Lecoq learned from Hanover that the road through Neustadt, Lüneburg and Artlenburg was still free of the enemy; at Münder a spy told him that the enemy held Braunschweig with numerous cavalry and raided as far as Ohof, as Hiller also learned at Neustadt, and from the newspapers he learned of the enemy's rapid advance towards Berlin and of the King of Holland's approach to the Weser. On 7 November Lieutenant Massow's outposts reported the enemy's advance on the road from Lemgo, and on the 8th Lecoq reconnoitred the enemy. Loison's letter gave the position of the various Prussian corps and the surrender of Stettin, Küstrin etc., and the protocol required that an officer first be sent to the Elbe to verify the circumstances stated. The King's summons of the 12th brought the news of the fall of Magdeburg and Napoleon's army order on Ratkau; Lecoq rode to the enemy camp partly to reconnoitre the enemy, and Michaud's letter repeated the news of the morning and allowed the commandant to send an officer to General Blücher to verify it. Michaud then sent the Bulletins announcing the capitulations of Prenzlau, Stettin and Küstrin. On the 13th it was learned that the King of Holland had left with his guards and some other regiments, and that the division of Mortier's corps was said to have marched towards Hamburg earlier; later it was known for certain that the enemy had moved down the Weser with a great part of his forces and almost entirely evacuated the left bank, and Lecoq estimated the enemy left behind at only 6000 men. On the 18th dü Monceau wrote that Napoleon was angered at the Prussian generals' conduct, and Lecoq answered that they had full knowledge of the Prussian army's misfortune and counted on no relief. On the 19th the Prince of Waldeck told the generals all he knew of the Prussian army, that the French had already crossed the Vistula, so that Prussia was irretrievably lost, and that Italian troops had arrived at Pyrmont to reinforce the blockading troops; this news wholly discouraged the generals. Savary wrote that the King of Prussia had not a battalion left and was himself in flight, and on the 20th repeated the story of the Prussian state's misfortunes, adding the lie that Glogau and Breslau had already capitulated.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images. Höpfner calls Savary's statement on Glogau and Breslau a lie; it is kept as his. The passages read do not show whether anyone at Hameln knew of the suspension of arms of 16 November, whose article 4 named Hameln and Nienburg (claim side-a-objectives). Pages 351-352 and 366, on Lecoq's march and on the days after the 13th, were not read. English renderings (ours): 'when, however, on the evening of the 25th he received news from Hanover that the road through Neustadt, Lüneburg and Artlenburg was still free of the enemy, he suddenly resolved once more to withdraw across the Elbe, and that same night sent Captain Hiller ahead to prepare the march on that line'; 'at Münder General Lecoq received from a spy the news that the enemy had occupied Braunschweig with numerous cavalry and was raiding as far as Ohof; news that Captain Hiller had also received at Neustadt'; 'when the general now also saw from the newspapers the enemy's rapid advance in the direction of Berlin and learned of the King of Holland's approach to the Weser, he gave his' (the sentence continues on p. 351, which was not read); 'on 7 November at 1 o'clock Lieutenant Massow, who stood on outpost with 60 dragoons and 10 hussars, reported that the enemy was advancing on the road from Lemgo and that his posts this side of Aerzen were being pushed back by superior enemy cavalry'; 'on 8 November General Lecoq reconnoitred the enemy and the enemy the fortress, which led to an insignificant cannonade'; 'it was General of Division Loison, who brought a letter from the King of Holland to General Lecoq, in which he summoned him, communicating the position of the various Prussian corps and the surrender of Stettin, Küstrin etc., to capitulate in return for free withdrawal, but in case of refusal threatened to reduce the town to ashes in 24 hours and to lay all the resulting misfortune on the general'; 'in a protocol signed by all it was unanimously declared that the free withdrawal was to be accepted, since in the prevailing circumstances a corps of 9000 men must be dearer to the King than holding so remote a fortress, which must in any case fall in 2 months at the latest; but before the capitulation was concluded an officer was to be sent to the Elbe to convince himself of the truth of the circumstances stated'; 'on the ground of General Brack's failure to return, the King of Holland on the 12th sent a parlementaire anew, complained in serious words of that general's detention, and at the same time summoned the commandant and the generals of the garrison to surrender the fortress in two hours if they did not wish to be treated with all severity'; 'to impress them still more, the news of the fall of Magdeburg and the army order in which Napoleon praises the marshals who had pursued Blücher's corps and forced it to capitulate at Ratkau were attached to the summons'; 'the colonel accepted the invitation, while General Lecoq rode with Captain Hiller and Lieutenant Below to the enemy camp, to obtain good terms of capitulation if possible and at the same time to reconnoitre the enemy'; 'the letter contained nothing but the repetition of the news from the theatre of war already communicated in the morning, with the addition that after such events it was unreasonable still to want to defend the fortress, but that the commandant was permitted to send an officer to General Blücher to convince himself of the truth of what had been communicated, though after this officer's return the fortress must then be surrendered and the garrison become prisoners of war'; 'General Michaud announced by a parlementaire that the King of Holland had left for another destination, and that he, the general, had taken over the chief command. At the same time he sent the Bulletins that announced the unhappy capitulations of Prenzlau, Stettin and Küstrin'; 'also on the 13th many movements were seen in the enemy camps, and it was soon learned that with the King of Holland his guards and some other regiments had also left, as the division of Mortier's corps was said to have left the neighbourhood of Hameln earlier and marched on towards Hamburg, since Napoleon had ordered from Berlin under 6 November that Marshal Mortier should work together with Marshals Soult and Bernadotte for the destruction of Blücher's corps and march on Hamburg to oppose the Prussians' crossing there'; 'it was now known for certain that the enemy had moved off down the Weser with a great part of his forces and had almost entirely evacuated the left bank. General Lecoq himself estimated the enemy left behind at only 6000 men. His camp was seen in the area this side of Fischbeck'; 'on the 18th the garrison of Fort George was relieved by the 1st battalion Oranien and the 3rd battalion of Schenk, since it had many sick from the damp casemates and the fort had no hospital'; 'the letter contained the notice that Napoleon was angered in the highest degree at the conduct of the Prussian generals and had ordered that they be treated with the utmost severity, and that no capitulation be granted them any more if they did not surrender the fortress forthwith'; 'when Colonel Stedtmann, on being asked, named the garrison's captivity as the main condition, General Lecoq, who had command of the French language, as the commandant had not, drew up a letter in which he told General dü Monceau that they had indeed full knowledge of the misfortune of the Prussian army and so counted on no relief, but that they nevertheless meant, in duty, to hold the fortress until all means of defence were exhausted or all provisions consumed; if, therefore, General dü Monceau really intended to spare the town, the commandant would hand over the fortress on 20 December, provided no relief had arrived by then;'; 'on the 19th in the afternoon the Prince of Waldeck came to Hameln and told the generals everything he knew of the events in the Prussian army, assured them also that the French had already crossed the Vistula, so that Prussia was irretrievably lost. He further said that Italian troops had already arrived at Pyrmont to reinforce the blockading troops'; 'this news, communicated by a prince attached to the Prussian state, wholly discouraged the generals, while in public they still prepared everything for a serious defence and held a conference on it with the artillery and engineer officers'; 'it was Captain Charles with a letter from General Savary, in which he announced to the commandant his arrival as commander of the besieging corps, and at the same time expressed his pleasure at the commandant's sensible views of the state of affairs, adding that he nevertheless could not accept the conditions put, since the King of Prussia had not a battalion left and was himself in flight; he wished to settle the rest orally, and left it to them to fix the time and place for it'; 'at first the Prussian generals refused the meeting, but at last agreed to fix the rendezvous for the 20th at 9 o'clock in the morning at the Wehrberg Warte'; 'the French general received the Prussian generals very brusquely, told them in his Emperor's name that the last moment for capitulation had come, that later nothing more would be ag-'; 'reed to; he repeated the story of all the misfortune that had struck the Prussian state, and added the lie that Glogau and Breslau had already capitulated'.

claims.value: Side A (French): on 31 October the Emperor wrote to the King of Holland that Hameln and Nienburg would soon surrender when they learned of their country's disasters, and that he should put a small corps of observation before them, without blockading them, to keep them from raiding the country; on 7 November he told Mortier to leave a small corps before Hameln and Nienburg and to move into Lauenburg and on Hamburg, in pursuit of Blücher's column. The 29th Bulletin, of 9 November: Mortier had set out for Hanover and Hamburg with his army corps, and the King of Holland had had Hameln blockaded. Mortier wrote on 12 November that he had moved on Hameln by the King's order to surround it on the right bank, and would leave two small corps to observe Hameln and Nienburg as the Emperor prescribed; on 13 November, that he was ordering Dumonceau to leave troops in observation before both. The 32nd Bulletin, of 16 November: Mortier had arrived with the 8th corps at Hamburg to close the Elbe and the Weser, and Savary had been charged with the blockade of Hameln with the Dutch division. By Höpfner, Napoleon ordered Mortier on 13 November to set about the investment of Hameln in earnest, with two bridges over the Weser and the blockading troops properly entrenched against sorties, Rinteln to serve as base and supply the guns for the attack; and on 18 November ordered Savary to Hameln to take command of the blockading troops, the guns from Rinteln to bombard the place to hasten its surrender, and the garrison to be granted a capitulation as prisoners of war, the officers released on parole and the private soldiers transported to France. The King of Holland first summoned the garrison through Loison to capitulate in return for free withdrawal, and approved free withdrawal as the main point, then on the 12th demanded surrender and refused Lecoq any terms but captivity. The suspension of arms signed at Charlottenburg on 16 November, which the 33rd Bulletin, of 17 November, prints, provided in article 4 that Hameln and Nienburg, with the places named in article 2, would be handed over to the French troops with their armament and munitions within the eight days following the exchange of ratifications, their garrisons not to be prisoners of war but directed on Kœnigsberg; ratifications were to be exchanged at Graudenz at the latest on the 21st, and by Foucart's note hostilities were to cease only then. The 35th Bulletin, of 28 November, says the King of Prussia told Duroc at Osterode that he could not ratify it.
claims.rationale: The Emperor's and Mortier's letters and the Bulletins, read from the page images, with Höpfner's summary of Napoleon's orders of 13 and 18 November, which were not seen in Foucart. The aims moved from observation without blockade (31 October) to blockade (9 and 16 November) and to investment, bombardment and a capitulation as prisoners of war (13 and 18 November, by Höpfner); they came from the Emperor and from the commanders before Hameln, so the phase is left unresolved. The capitulation of 20 November made the garrison prisoners of war (claim capitulation), while the suspension of arms, had it been ratified, would have sent it to Kœnigsberg (our comparison); the passages read do not show whether anyone before Hameln knew of the suspension. The sentence on hostilities is Foucart's note, not the suspension's text. English renderings (ours): 'the Emperor to the King of Holland. Berlin, 31 October 1806'; 'Hameln and Nienburg will not be slow to surrender when they learn of the disasters of their country. Put a small corps of observation before them, without blockading them, to prevent them from making raids in the country'; 'the Emperor to Marshal Mortier. Berlin, 7 November 1806'; 'you will leave a small corps before Hameln and Nienburg and will move into Lauenburg and from there on Hamburg, from where, according to the orders I would send you, you would move into Swedish Pomerania in pursuit of General Blücher's column'; '29th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Berlin, 9 November 1806'; 'Marshal Mortier has set out for Hanover and for Hamburg with his army corps'; 'the King of Holland has had Hameln blockaded'; 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 12 November 1806'; 'I moved on Hameln, by the King of Holland's order, to surround that strong place on the right bank of the Weser'; 'I shall leave two small corps to observe Hameln and Nienburg as you prescribe to me'; 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 13 November 1806'; 'I am giving orders for General Dumonceau to leave in observation, both before Hameln and before Nienburg, the 2nd and 3rd light infantry regiments, the 7th of the line, the 2nd of cavalry, all Dutch troops'; '32nd Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 16 November 1806'; 'Marshal Mortier has arrived with the 8th corps at Hamburg to close the Elbe and the Weser'; 'General Savary has been charged with the blockade of Hameln with the Dutch division'; 'under 13 November Napoleon had ordered Marshal Mortier now to set about the investment of Hameln in earnest, to have two bridges thrown over the Weser and to arrange for the blockading troops to entrench themselves properly so as to be safe against any sortie; Rinteln was to serve them as a base and supply the guns for the attack; the Dutch corps, about 6000 men strong, seemed sufficient to be safe against the garrison if properly entrenched'; 'under 18 November Napoleon at last directed General Savary from Berlin to leave at once and go before Hameln to take command of the blockading troops; the guns from Rinteln were to bombard the place and so hasten its surrender, the field guns to defend the entrenchments; the 12th light infantry regiment was already on its way from Kassel as reinforcement; the commandant there, General Lagrange, was further to be asked to send off some cavalry; the garrison of Hameln could be granted a capitulation by which it would be prisoners of war, the officers released on parole, but the private soldiers transported to France etc.'; 'it was General of Division Loison, who brought a letter from the King of Holland to General Lecoq, in which he summoned him, communicating the position of the various Prussian corps and the surrender of Stettin, Küstrin etc., to capitulate in return for free withdrawal, but in case of refusal threatened to reduce the town to ashes in 24 hours and to lay all the resulting misfortune on the general'; 'he was very kindly received; the King approved the main point: that the garrison could go by the nearest road to the King's army; but referred him for the details to General Loison and Colonel Brüne'; 'on the ground of General Brack's failure to return, the King of Holland on the 12th sent a parlementaire anew, complained in serious words of that general's detention, and at the same time summoned the commandant and the generals of the garrison to surrender the fortress in two hours if they did not wish to be treated with all severity'; 'the King refused to receive the general, and only had him told that the garrison must now in any case surrender as prisoners of war. General Lecoq rejected this condition, but allowed a French officer to accompany him to Hameln with a letter from General Michaud to the commandant, where he was let in in the evening without blindfold'; '1. 33rd Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 17 November 1806' (the '1.' is the footnote's mark); 'the attached suspension of arms was signed yesterday at Charlottenburg'; 'Art. 4. — The places of Hameln and Nienburg, as well as those designated in article 2, shall be handed over to the French troops with their armament and munitions, of which an inventory shall be drawn up, within the eight days following the exchange of the ratifications of the present suspension of arms. The garrisons of these places shall not be prisoners of war; they shall be directed on Kœnigsberg, and they shall be given every facility necessary for this'; 'Art. 6. — The present suspension of arms shall be ratified by the two high contracting powers, and the exchange of ratifications shall take place at Graudenz at the latest on the 21st of the present month'; 'done at Charlottenburg, 16 November 1806'; 'hostilities were to cease only at the moment of the exchange of ratifications'; '35th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Posen, 28 November 1806'; 'the marshal of the palace, Duroc, went as far as Osterode, where he saw the King of Prussia, who declared to him that part of his states was occupied by the Russians and that he was entirely in their dependence; that consequently he could not ratify the suspension of arms that his plenipotentiaries had concluded, because he could not carry out its stipulations'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: on 13 August the order came to put Hameln in a state of defence. Lecoq resolved on the evening of the 25th to withdraw across the Elbe, while General Hagken proposed falling on the rear of the troops blockading Magdeburg or marching through unoccupied Saxony to Silesia; a council of Lecoq's commanders later judged the corps's departure from Hameln no longer advisable. After Loison's summons Lecoq held himself bound to accept free withdrawal to the King's army for his troops, and the protocol held that a corps of 9000 men must be dearer to the King than holding so remote a fortress, which must fall in 2 months at the latest. Lecoq wrote to the commandant that the King perhaps expected a serious defence; Caprivi would in no case give up the fort just like that; when the King of Holland demanded surrender as prisoners of war, Lecoq rejected it, the commandant answered that there would be time to think of capitulating when all means of defence were exhausted, and a serious defence was announced; the commandant promised Caprivi not to negotiate before 20 December. On the 18th Lecoq wrote that, though they counted on no relief, they meant in duty to hold the fortress until all means of defence were exhausted or all provisions consumed, and offered that the commandant would hand it over on 20 December if no relief had come. Lecoq's draft capitulation commended to the new monarch's favour the officers from provinces that might be ceded at the peace. Senior officers urged Wedell to oppose the capitulation, and the men of the regiment Hagken and of the 3rd battalions mutinied after it was made known. Höpfner: everything seemed to invite a sortie, given the superiority over the enemy, yet they contented themselves with Hiller's attempt to bring in guns; and he holds that a commandant knows no consideration other than the preservation of his fortress.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images. The aims shifted between withdrawal, free withdrawal, defence, delay and capitulation; they came from the orders the fortress had received and from its commanders' decisions, so the phase is left unresolved. The passages read give no order to the garrison after that of 13 August and no instruction from the King after Jena. The sentence on the commandant's duty is Höpfner's judgement. English renderings (ours): 'on 13 August the order arrived to put Hameln in a state of defence'; 'when, however, on the evening of the 25th he received news from Hanover that the road through Neustadt, Lüneburg and Artlenburg was still free of the enemy, he suddenly resolved once more to withdraw across the Elbe, and that same night sent Captain Hiller ahead to prepare the march on that line'; 'on the 26th he already set out with the corps for Münder and Lauenau, the advance guard for Neustadt, without informing General Hagken, who had wanted to join him and had proposed falling on the rear of the troops blockading Magdeburg or marching through unoccupied Saxony to Silesia'; 'thereupon General Lecoq called together General Wedell and the commanders of his corps, and put to them the question whether the corps's departure from Hameln was still advisable, since the enemy was already approaching. The answer was in the negative'; 'General Lecoq held himself obliged to accept a free withdrawal to the King's army for the troops under his command; but unless the commandant joined in this capitulation, General Loison would agree to nothing'; 'in a protocol signed by all it was unanimously declared that the free withdrawal was to be accepted, since in the prevailing circumstances a corps of 9000 men must be dearer to the King than holding so remote a fortress, which must in any case fall in 2 months at the latest; but before the capitulation was concluded an officer was to be sent to the Elbe to convince himself of the truth of the circumstances stated'; 'even General Lecoq wrote to the commandant that he should by no means be hasty with the surrender of the fortress, since the King perhaps expected a serious defence after all'; 'when the latter thereupon gave him a sharp reprimand in a letter, and declared at the same time that he was commandant of the fortress and the fort only a part of it, the colonel answered that he had acted according to duty and conscience and would in no case give up the fort just like that'; 'the King refused to receive the general, and only had him told that the garrison must now in any case surrender as prisoners of war. General Lecoq rejected this condition, but allowed a French officer to accompany him to Hameln with a letter from General Michaud to the commandant, where he was let in in the evening without blindfold'; 'to this letter the commandant answered, since none of the commanders considered a capitulation justified under the conditions it contained, and Colonel Caprivi in particular spoke out vehemently against it, that under the conditions given there would still be time to think of a capitulation when all means of defence were exhausted'; 'to quiet the garrison's discontent at the many negotiations, it was formally announced that every capitulation had been broken off and that a serious defence would be made'; 'on the 13th an inventory of all stores was taken, and it turned out that with the most ample rations the provisions would last until 20 December, whereupon the commandant gave Colonel Caprivi the promise, before this'; 'day, not to enter into any negotiation with the enemy'; 'on the 18th the garrison of Fort George was relieved by the 1st battalion Oranien and the 3rd battalion of Schenk, since it had many sick from the damp casemates and the fort had no hospital'; 'when Colonel Stedtmann, on being asked, named the garrison's captivity as the main condition, General Lecoq, who had command of the French language, as the commandant had not, drew up a letter in which he told General dü Monceau that they had indeed full knowledge of the misfortune of the Prussian army and so counted on no relief, but that they nevertheless meant, in duty, to hold the fortress until all means of defence were exhausted or all provisions consumed; if, therefore, General dü Monceau really intended to spare the town, the commandant would hand over the fortress on 20 December, provided no relief had arrived by then;'; 'the 5th article of the draft capitulation, as General Leeoq had drawn it up, commended the officers who belonged to provinces that might be ceded at the peace to the favour of the new monarch with regard to their maintenance in case of invalidity; it was rejected by the French as inadmissible'; 'already in the morning some senior officers had suspected what was going on outside, and had spoken of it with General Wedell at the parole; Major Eller, commander of the 3rd battalion of Hagken, Colonel Renzel, commander of the 3rd battalion of Schenk, and Colonel Oertel, commander of the infantry regiment Lettow, had called on the general to oppose the capitulation, but he had given the answer: "Do you not know Prussian subordination? That is the business of the commandant and of General Lecoq; they have to answer for everything."'; 'the men of the regiment Hagken and of the 3rd battalions broke open the magazines, got drunk, scattered or sold the provisions, fired their muskets in the streets, especially against the commandant's house,'; 'the wooded ground up to there was perfectly known, and everything seemed to invite a sortie, given the superiority over the enemy, since the enemy's cavalry was not to be feared in the broken ground'; 'nevertheless they contented themselves with allowing Captain Hiller, at his request, to advance on the left bank of the Weser to try to bring into the fortress some guns that the enemy had left standing near Hemeringen. For this purpose he received a hundred volunteer marksmen of the infantry regiment Lettow and 16 hussars,' (the sentence continues on p. 368, which was not read); 'all the excuses brought forward for the capitulation that were taken from the fortress's situation come to nothing in view of the strong garrison, well equipped with everything; the reasons based on the political situation of the state were even more reprehensible; the commandant knows no other consideration than the preservation of his fortress'.
