claims.value: Side A (French) attacked: Bodart has the French under Savary force the garrison to capitulate after a 14-day blockade, and the 29th Bulletin says the King of Holland had had Hameln blockaded. Höpfner: on 7 November the enemy advanced on the road from Lemgo with superior cavalry; Lieutenant Treskow with 70 fusiliers and 10 Jäger held the exits of Gr. Berkel and Lieutenant Massow posted the dragoons to the right of the village, but a cavalry brigade forced them back on Kl. Berkel, where a company of the battalion of Oranien received the pursuing cavalry with volleys, and the investment on the left bank was completed that day. On the 9th the enemy bridged the Weser at Ohr and drove the post at the Afferde Warte back to the barrier, and on the 10th Mortier's troops attacked the covered way at the Mühlen gate with tirailleurs. Mortier: on the 10th all the enemy posts were driven into the place. The King of Holland summoned the fortress through Loison and again on the 12th, and Savary refused the garrison's conditions on the 19th and pressed for its capitulation on the 20th. Side B's actions were the reception of its outposts, the reoccupation of the inundation redoubt the enemy had left and Captain Hiller's attempt on the left bank to bring in guns the enemy had left near Hemeringen; Höpfner says everything seemed to invite a sortie, yet the commanders contented themselves with Hiller's attempt.
claims.rationale: Coded A_attacked: side A invested and summoned the fortress and side B capitulated; side B's small actions were within the blockade and do not make it an attacker. The phase is left unresolved: the blockade followed the orders of the King of Holland and the Emperor, while the attacks, summonses and demands were the commanders' own (claims side-a-command, side-a-objectives). The outcome of Hiller's attempt, on p. 368, was not read. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; '29th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Berlin, 9 November 1806'; 'the King of Holland has had Hameln blockaded'; 'on 7 November at 1 o'clock Lieutenant Massow, who stood on outpost with 60 dragoons and 10 hussars, reported that the enemy was advancing on the road from Lemgo and that his posts this side of Aerzen were being pushed back by superior enemy cavalry'; 'before this support could arrive, the outpost officers had taken their measures; Lieutenant Treskow with 70 fusiliers and 10 Jäger had occupied the exits of Gr. Berkel, Lieutenant Massow had posted himself with the dragoons to the right of the village'; 'the enemy soon advanced with a cavalry brigade — a Dutch Guard dragoon regiment and a hussar regiment — and forced the Prussian officers to retreat on Kl. Berkel'; 'the battalion of Oranien and the two horse-artillery guns had posted themselves on the height behind the Berkel Warte; one company pushed forward to behind the Warte'; 'this company received the pursuing enemy cavalry with several well-aimed volleys, by which, as also by the fire of the horse artillery and of the guns of Fort No. I, it lost some men and withdrew'; 'an enemy column was seen marching towards the Weser and going into bivouacs; and by the occupation of the wood between Berkel and Hemeringen the investment of the fortress on the left bank was completed that same day'; 'on the 9th the enemy, under the protection of a howitzer battery set up on the Ohrberg, threw a bridge over the Weser at Ohr, for which the boats had been brought downstream'; 'the Prussian post at the Afferde Warte was at once attacked in superior force and, though reinforced from the fortress, pushed back to the barrier'; 'on 10 November part of Mortier's corps also appeared before Hameln'; 'an enemy column moved from Rehrsen to the Baßberg and attacked the covered way with tirailleurs, who posted themselves in the gardens and garden houses in front and for a long time kept up their fire with the garrison of the covered way at the Mühlen gate'; 'it was General of Division Loison, who brought a letter from the King of Holland to General Lecoq, in which he summoned him, communicating the position of the various Prussian corps and the surrender of Stettin, Küstrin etc., to capitulate in return for free withdrawal, but in case of refusal threatened to reduce the town to ashes in 24 hours and to lay all the resulting misfortune on the general'; 'on the ground of General Brack's failure to return, the King of Holland on the 12th sent a parlementaire anew, complained in serious words of that general's detention, and at the same time summoned the commandant and the generals of the garrison to surrender the fortress in two hours if they did not wish to be treated with all severity'; 'quite unexpectedly a parlementaire was again announced on the evening of the 19th'; 'it was Captain Charles with a letter from General Savary, in which he announced to the commandant his arrival as commander of the besieging corps, and at the same time expressed his pleasure at the commandant's sensible views of the state of affairs, adding that he nevertheless could not accept the conditions put, since the King of Prussia had not a battalion left and was himself in flight; he wished to settle the rest orally, and left it to them to fix the time and place for it'; 'at first the Prussian generals refused the meeting, but at last agreed to fix the rendezvous for the 20th at 9 o'clock in the morning at the Wehrberg Warte'; 'the French general received the Prussian generals very brusquely, told them in his Emperor's name that the last moment for capitulation had come, that later nothing more would be ag-'; 'later the enemy left the redoubt of his own accord, and it was at once reoccupied by the garrison, since it was considered well placed for sending patrols from it to the Afferde Warte'; 'the wooded ground up to there was perfectly known, and everything seemed to invite a sortie, given the superiority over the enemy, since the enemy's cavalry was not to be feared in the broken ground'; 'nevertheless they contented themselves with allowing Captain Hiller, at his request, to advance on the left bank of the Weser to try to bring into the fortress some guns that the enemy had left standing near Hemeringen. For this purpose he received a hundred volunteer marksmen of the infantry regiment Lettow and 16 hussars,' (the sentence continues on p. 368, which was not read); 'Marshal Mortier to the Emperor. Hanover, 12 November 1806'; 'on the evening of the 9th I debouched by Hastenbeck; on the 10th, in the course of the day, all the enemy posts were driven back into the place and dislodged from the brick fort situated on the Hamel, at half range from the town'.

claims.value: Side B held a permanent fortress: Höpfner describes the town's bastioned land front with its main ditch, ravelins, covered way and lunettes, the fortified island of the Werder, the bridgehead's flèches, the inundation of the Hamelbach, and Fort George's three forts with their mine galleries and the two redoubts linking them to the bridgehead. After the Prussians took possession, the casemates in the town and the fort were cleared, the breastworks improved, the palisading restored and the inundation sluice repaired and covered by a small redoubt 1300 paces from the fortress; the Weser was blocked by trees above and below, and a new coupure under the Klütberg was covered by a breastwork with gun embrasures. Lecoq's camp at the foot of the Klütberg was entrenched from 24 October. In the night to the 10th the inundation redoubt was abandoned, and later the redoubts were abandoned and the coupure in the gorge closed. For side A, Napoleon's order of 13 November, as Höpfner gives it, required the blockading troops to entrench properly against any sortie, and his order of 18 November had the field guns defend the entrenchments; Schöler held at the capitulation that the enemy was protected against sorties by the inundation. No passage read describes side A's works.
claims.rationale: Coded B_fortified: side B defended permanent works, readied before the investment, and Lecoq's camp was entrenched before it, so the claim is tagged inherited. Napoleon's orders as Höpfner gives them required side A to entrench, and the order of 18 November speaks of its entrenchments, but no passage read shows them made; a coding that counted them would give both_fortified. English renderings (ours): 'the fortress of Hameln on the right bank of the Weser was fortified on the land side by a detached bastion and 8 bastions, a fausse-braye, a broad and deep main ditch watered by the Hamelbach, with small ravelins, covered way and advanced ditch; lunettes lay before the detached bastion at the lower junction with the Weser and before the 3 gate ravelins'; 'the water side of the fortress was only badly defended, by a fortified island, the Werder'; 'the bridge was defended by a large flèche, flanked by 2 small flèches with ditches and covered way'; 'on the right bank of the Weser the valley heights, namely the Baßberg, come within 1000 paces of the town. Except for the somewhat higher ground before the Oster gate, the whole valley floor could be flooded by the Hamelbach, for which purpose a sluice had been built in the brook 1600 paces south-east of the fortress'; 'on the south-eastern tip of the Klütberg lay Fort George, consisting of three separate forts: No. I on the summit, No. II lower but still on the ridge, No. III on the slope towards the Weser; all three linked by an open communication, Nos. II and III also by an underground one'; 'before No. I on the hill side and before No. III towards the Weser lay mine galleries'; 'two redoubts lying half-way secured the link between Fort George and the bridgehead'; 'when the Prussians took possession of Hameln the fortress was in a very bad state, but work on it had begun actively at once'; 'the casemates in the town and in the fort were cleared, the breastworks improved, the palisading restored, the inundation sluice put in usable condition, and a small redoubt built to cover it, 1300 paces from the fortress, the Weser above and be-'; 'low blocked by trees, a new coupure made under the Klütberg and covered by a breastwork with gun embrasures, and in front of it a broken breastwork carried up to a small height to link with Fort III, which lay wholly under the fort's fire'; 'on 24 October General Lecoq led his corps into a camp at the foot of the Klütberg, and had its entrenchment begun at once'; 'in the night to the 10th the new, though faultily laid-out, inundation redoubt on the right bank of the Weser was abandoned on the commandant's order, since in his opinion it was useless, because the inundation could no longer be drained. The enemy occupied it at once'; 'besides the 2nd battalion of Oranien, the 4 companies of the 2nd battalion of vac. Grävenitz were now also moved to Fort George. The redoubts were abandoned as soon as the camp's magazines had been cleared; on the other hand the coupure in the gorge was closed and its defence also entrusted to Colonel Caprivi'; 'under 13 November Napoleon had ordered Marshal Mortier now to set about the investment of Hameln in earnest, to have two bridges thrown over the Weser and to arrange for the blockading troops to entrench themselves properly so as to be safe against any sortie; Rinteln was to serve them as a base and supply the guns for the attack; the Dutch corps, about 6000 men strong, seemed sufficient to be safe against the garrison if properly entrenched'; 'under 18 November Napoleon at last directed General Savary from Berlin to leave at once and go before Hameln to take command of the blockading troops; the guns from Rinteln were to bombard the place and so hasten its surrender, the field guns to defend the entrenchments; the 12th light infantry regiment was already on its way from Kassel as reinforcement; the commandant there, General Lagrange, was further to be asked to send off some cavalry; the garrison of Hameln could be granted a capitulation by which it would be prisoners of war, the officers released on parole, but the private soldiers transported to France etc.'; 'all were silent, and as General Savary pressed General Schöler to declare himself, the latter in fact believed that nothing else remained for him but to capitulate, since the enemy stood on the Baßberg only 900 paces from the covered way and was protected against sorties by the inundation, while a bombardment could easily reduce the town, and with it the magazines, which were not bombproof, to ashes, and so on'.

open_questions: Deferred: Höpfner, Bd. 2, pp. 351-352, 354-356, 362, 366, 368, 374 (Lecoq's march and return; the French movements in western Germany; the beginning of Major Beaufort's remonstrance; part of the days between the 13th and the 18th, with the end of Captain Hiller's attempt; and the officers' letter of the night of 20 November, which Savary's of the 21st answered), and the parts of pp. 376-378 not transcribed, among them the paragraphs on the pay and the garrison's chests; seen only in the OCR, the passages naming Hameln in Foucart t. II at pp. 75, 346, 749, 795, 831, among them the Emperor's view that Hameln's garrison was not strong, his order to occupy Rinteln to observe Hameln and his remark of 9 November that the corps that had left Hameln may have gone out to forage; General Savary's report and Napoleon's orders of 13 and 18 November, known here only from Höpfner's summary and not found in the Foucart pages read; and the capitulation's text. No figure seen only in the OCR is restated.

Most consequential gap: side A's strength at the capitulation. Bodart's 6,000, Höpfner's 'only 6000', Lecoq's estimate of 6000 and the 'about 6000' of Napoleon's order of 13 November as Höpfner gives it are the only totals for the blockading force, and none is shown to be a count; Mortier gives the divisions Dumonceau and Michaud as about 7,000 men on 12 November, before Michaud's division was called away, and calls the Dutch corps left in observation weak, without a return. A return of the troops before Hameln for 18 to 20 November, such as General Savary's report or the King of Holland's correspondence, could close it.

Disputes kept as separate claims or within them: the garrison (over 5000 in the garrison and 4000 in Lecoq's corps, the protocol's 9000, and 9—10,000 and almost 10,000 after the capitulation, Höpfner; 10,000, Bodart; 7,000 camped under the walls, the King of Holland on 9 November; 10,000 at Hameln and Nienburg together, Mortier on 13 November); the guns (Höpfner's 93, 46, 21 and 15 without the unserviceable ones; Bodart's 129); the prisoners (about 600, Höpfner and Bodart; 6000, General Savary's report as Höpfner gives it); Savary's charge (already in the 32nd Bulletin of 16 November; by Napoleon's order of 18 November and announced on the 19th, Höpfner); the brick fort on the Hamel (its posts dislodged on the 10th, Mortier; the inundation redoubt abandoned on the commandant's order in the night to the 10th, Höpfner, if it is the same work); the French divisions before Hameln (Gobert and Michaud, Höpfner; Dumonceau and Michaud, Mortier); and the surrender of Glogau and Breslau, which Savary asserted on the 20th and Höpfner calls a lie.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked; his 600 prisoners and 10,000 garrison agree with Höpfner's figures and his 6,000 with Höpfner's for the enemy, but his 129 guns do not); Foucart, Campagne de Prusse, t. II, and Campagne de Pologne, t. I, one family (the same author's editions of the French side's documents, from the page images: the Emperor's letters to the King of Holland of 22 and 31 October, to Mortier of 7 November and to Ney of 9 November, Mortier's letters to the Emperor of 12 and 13 November, the 29th, 32nd, 33rd and 35th Bulletins, and the suspension of arms of 16 November printed with the 33rd, with Foucart's note on it); Höpfner, Bd. 2, 2nd edition (the Prussian side's history; in this section he gives Napoleon's orders of 13 and 18 November and the French commanders' letters in summary, cites General Savary's report for the prisoners and an enemy officer's statement for the French loss of 7 November, and says that as good as nothing about the enemy's movements in western Germany has been communicated from the French side, so his French-side details rest on documents he does not name).
